## API docs for events!

*2020-07-28 to 2022-04-14 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/API.20docs.20for.20events.21/with/960879)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-28 22:37 UTC

We now have the beginnings of API documentation for events.  you can see it here in e.g.: 
https://chat.zulip.org/api/get-events#update_global_notifications

A few notes on where things are here:
* It's really cool to have these here in the documentation!
* The data is fully tested against the implementation, in the same way our other OpenAPI data is.
* However, it's very incomplete -- only a small subset of events are documented right now.
* The types for fields are present in the data; it's just the display logic (for all of our OpenAPI response data!) that doesn't have a place to put types.  We should figure out a solution for that.
* I suspect once this is completed, we'll end up with an infinitely long page; we may need to figure out a design with a dropdown or index or something to address that issue.
* I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed right now and it might make sense for someone else to take up some of the work of editing the descriptions and/or doing the design changes to show the types (or other details like `required`).
* E.g. https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/15956 documents several important event types but is hundreds of lines of new content.
* We still need to backfill copying in the **Changes** values from the API changelog.
* There's a few open questions about details like whether we should display the `type` and `id` documentation along every individual event or not.  I'm tempted to say yes for clarity; it doesn't add much to the total height given examples etc.

@*mobile* @*terminal* @Aditya Verma (orientor) FYI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-28 22:39 UTC

Oh, and finally, there's probably a discussion we will want to have about improving the format of various event types that are likely not used by mobile/terminal yet but might be in the future (E.g. various settings-change events) to be more consistent.  But that probably belongs on another thread for later; just mentioning it to get folks thinking.

**Greg Price** · 2020-07-29 06:27 UTC

* Another specific bit in the data that stuck out at me:

  For `realm_user` with op `add`, the description for `bot_type` says it's `null` if the user isn't a bot.

  But in the example, the user isn't a bot and `bot_type` isn't `null` -- instead it's absent. (Which seems like the better API choice to me in the first place.)

  For anyone coming at this from a Python perspective, it's worth pointing out that this difference is more conspicuous in JS than it would be in Python. In Python, a JSON `null` typically translates to `None`, which is also the value you get if you look for a dictionary item that isn't there, so a JSON property that's absent is almost like one with the value `null`. But in JS, `null` is one value and `undefined` is a different value, and if you look for an object property that isn't there you get `undefined`, not `null`.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-30 19:21 UTC

One major design choice that Stripe has made in their docs is that the entire thing is a single page.

That has some nice benefits -- it makes it easier to search or browse through and find something, when you don't already know exactly what you're looking for.

I think design choices like how each section is collapsed to a summary, with a "show" button to expand it, are to a large extent driven by that one. They're helpful in that context, to help you browse.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-30 19:27 UTC

One thing that the Stripe design makes me think about is that our longest pages, like https://zulip.com/api/get-events , are pretty tough to browse. There's probably a few things we can do there.

One possible option would be to have each event collapsed initially to just its name and one-sentence description. We'd have a button to expand any given event, and a "Show all" at the top to expand all of them. That would probably be pretty helpful.

Another thing we could do is add an index at the top. If we did the thing with summaries and show-all, this would be redundant. But if we don't do that, then a separate index would be quite helpful. Basically it makes a separate always-collapsed copy of the list, instead of making the items collapsible/expandable in place.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-30 19:33 UTC

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/46/veT0ewEL9NRjD3Q8wf9xnKAT/image.png)

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-27 06:45 UTC

I think that's also perhaps at the root of the difficulty with the icon. If the whole card, or whole top of the card, is the target, then the icon doesn't need to be inside a button (and probably shouldn't be.)

Common designs include:
* A down/up chevron at the end of the heading row. Material Design does this; search for "expand and collapse" [here](https://material.io/components/lists), or "expand a card" [here](https://material.io/components/cards).
* A right/down chevron, or triangle, at the start of the heading row (before the heading text). This is common in big nested trees, like in the Chrome dev tools' elements view.

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-27 06:48 UTC

## Emoji statuses in zulip.yaml

*2022-01-27 to 2022-04-15 · 51 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/Emoji.20statuses.20in.20zulip.2Eyaml/with/1317152)*

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-01-27 19:53 UTC

I think there's a bug in the API doc for the `user_status` part of the `/register` response.

```yaml
                      user_status:
                        allOf:
                          - $ref: "#/components/schemas/EmojiBase"
                        description: |
                          Present if `user_status` is present in `fetch_event_types`.

                          A dictionary which contains the [status](/help/status-and-availability)
                          of all users in the Zulip organization who have set a status.

                          **Changes**: The emoji parameters are new in Zulip 5.0 (feature level 86).
                          Previously, Zulip did not support emoji associated with statuses.

                          A status that does not have an emoji associated with it is encoded
                          with `emoji_name=""`.
                        additionalProperties:
                          description: |
                            `{user_id}`: Object containing the status details of a user
                            with the key of the object being the id of the user.
                          type: object
                          additionalProperties: false
                          properties:
                            away:
                              type: boolean
                              description: |
                                Whether the user has marked themself "away".
                            status_text:
                              type: string
                              description: |
                                The text content of the status message.
                            emoji_name:
                              type: string
                              description: |
                                The [emoji name](/api/add-reaction#parameters) for the emoji associated with the new status.

                                **Changes**: New in Zulip 5.0 (feature level 86).
                            emoji_code:
                              type: string
                              description: |
                                The [emoji code](/api/add-reaction#parameters) for the emoji associated with the new status.

                                **Changes**: New in Zulip 5.0 (feature level 86).
                            reaction_type:
                              type: string
                              description: |
                                The [emoji type](/api/add-reaction#parameters) for the emoji associated with the new status.

                                **Changes**: New in Zulip 5.0 (feature level 86).
```

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/a8/mgzhDY57WSpVealuETw9NrQe/image.png)

It correctly says that `user_status.{user_id}` is an "Object containing the status details of a user […]"

It incorrectly says that `user_status.emoji_code`, `user_status.emoji_name`, and `user_status.reaction_type` also exist.

I think this bug can be fixed by removing the following:

```yaml
                        allOf:
                          - $ref: "#/components/schemas/EmojiBase"
```

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-01-27 19:57 UTC

I also think that the part under `user_status.{user_id}` here, and the part for the data in a `user_status` event in `GET /events`, can be deduplicated. They have some slight differences that look accidental. I was thinking of making a `UserStatus` and `UserStatusBase` under `components/schemas`, following the pattern of, e.g., `EmojiReaction`/`EmojiReactionBase`.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-01-27 20:05 UTC

(I also think it's not quite appropriate for the descriptions of `user_status.{user_id}.emoji_name` and friends to link to `/api/add-reaction#parameters`, since they're about status emoji, not reaction emoji; same goes for the event.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-27 20:08 UTC

Those all seem right to me.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-27 20:10 UTC

The reference to EmojiBase looks like it intended to do some deduplication with other uses of emoji (in reactions?). But for that it should go a level deeper, where `emoji_name` and so on are.

And it's not so simple to do that deduplication, because of details like the "**Changes**" paragraph.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-27 20:11 UTC

The next question is what the actual behavior is. Does it match what you get if you delete the `allOf`?

```
                'allOf': [{'$ref': '#/components/schemas/UserStatusBase',
                           'nullable': False,
                           'x-scope': ['']},
                          {'additionalProperties': False,
```

This looks a lot like #16109. If that first schema `UserStatusBase` has any properties that aren't listed in the second branch of the `allOf`, then the resulting overall schema won't allow those properties. (And so if any of them are required by `UserStatusBase`, then the resulting overall schema will match no objects at all.)

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-02-01 21:55 UTC

> If that first schema `UserStatusBase` has any properties that aren't listed in the second branch of the `allOf`

But there aren't/weren't any such properties. Right? :thinking:

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-01 22:08 UTC

The problem was the `additionalProperties: false` you had left outside of the `allOf`. `additionalProperties` always refers to the properties defined as *direct siblings* in the schema tree. There were no such properties at that level (since you moved them into the `allOf`), so you were forbidding all properties.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-02-01 22:12 UTC

Ah OK, thanks! Luckily it looks like I did put an `additionalProperties: false` inside the second branch of the `allOf` (the branch that's not just `$ref: …`).

So with that, and with the one outside the `allOf` removed, it just ends up being a straightforward move from outside to inside the `allOf`, and that's appropriate, right?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-01 22:20 UTC

Yeah.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-02-04 01:38 UTC

I've actually just been experimenting more with the actual behavior of the API (without reading code), and I'm thinking we don't want to deduplicate the doc between `/register` and `/events` in this case, after all.

It seems that the meaning of a property's value, and whether a property is present or absent, can differ between `/register` and `/events`, as follows:

For `.away`:

| | `/register` | `/events` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `true` | user is unavailable | user is unavailable |
| `false` | N/A; doesn't happen? | user is available |
| missing | user is available | availability status not changed in this event; current value kept |

For `.status_text`:

| | `/register` | `/events` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| non-empty string, e.g., "foo" | status text is "foo" | status text is "foo" |
| empty string | N/A; doesn't happen? | there is no status text |
| missing | there is no status text | status text not changed in this event; current value kept |

For `.emoji_code`, `.emoji_name`, and `.reaction_type`:

| | `/register` | `/events` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| non-empty string | status emoji is as indicated | status emoji is as indicated |
| empty string | N/A; doesn't happen? | there is no status emoji |
| missing | there is no status emoji | status emoji not changed in this event; current value kept |

And in the `/register` case, if all properties  would be missing—`user_status.{user_id}.away`, `user_status.{user_id}.status_text`, and so on—then instead, with the same meaning, the entire object will be missing; there won't be anything at `user_status.{user_id}`.

We should find a nice way to present these findings in the doc, to the extent that they're accurate and not too strong as claims about servers' behavior. :smile:

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-08 04:41 UTC

In the documentation of the `muted_topics` event:
https://zulip.com/api/get-events#muted_topics
we say the data comes as an array of three-element tuples. We don't mention that older server versions send only a two-element tuple, without the timestamp.

Same thing at `muted_topics` in /api/register-queue.

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-08 04:41 UTC

I wanted to know what version that started with, because in general in mobile when we document some old server's behavior in our types, we want to have a comment mentioning the server version so we know when we can simplify away the old version.

Happily I didn't have to dig far, because /api/changelog does have the answer: it started at feature level 1, in Zulip 3.0.

The fact it was feature level 1 probably helps explain how we were missing the change notes where the feature is documented -- that was in the early days of our current set of practices for systematically documenting this stuff.

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-08 04:41 UTC

So, we should add an appropriate "**Changes**:" paragraph at `muted_topics` in /api/get-events and /api/register-queue.

Also there's a typo in /api/changelog (in an identifier, so it can potentially defeat a search): s/muted_topic/muted_topics/.

Just now I happened to run across one other small gap, which would be turned up by such an audit.

In feature level 58, part of Zulip 4.0, we gave set-typing-status support for stream messages. The changelog records that:
https://zulip.com/api/changelog

But the endpoint's own page doesn't:
https://zulip.com/api/set-typing-status#parameters
It just offers both options. It should have a **Changes** item on the `type` parameter.

(There is actually a mention of "new in Zulip 4.0" in the intro text at the top. **Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:02 UTC

I think one thing that's going on is that the newer format has a `name` field described like so:

> A unique, table, machine-readable name for the authentication method, intended to be used by clients with special behavior for specific authentication methods to correctly identify the method.

but then we never actually say what the values of that machine-readable name might be and what each one means. But then those same names (I'm 90% confident it's actually the same names -- again, we don't currently say) appear in `authentication_methods`. So the `authentication_methods` documentation doubles (though undocumentedly so) as a list of valid `name` values for `external_authentication_methods`, with a description for what each one means.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:03 UTC

If that's correct, then probably a good change would be to rearrange so that the description of the new-style thing, `external_authentication_methods`, contains that information. And have `authentication_methods` just refer to that.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:09 UTC

I'm a little bit tempted to say that these changes then don't need to be in the changelog or have "Changes:" paragraphs. In particular, with the new-style API here (i.e., `external_authentication_methods`), the client sees exactly the same thing when talking to
* a server too old to support OpenID Connect, or
* a server new enough to support OpenID Connect, but without having it set up and enabled.

## /server_settings: `realm_name`, etc.

*2022-02-22 to 2023-03-15 · 36 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/.2Fserver_settings.3A.20.60realm_name.60.2C.20etc.2E/with/1332888)*

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-02-22 21:27 UTC

I see the following comment in `api_get_server_settings`:

```py
    # IMPORTANT NOTE:
    # realm_name, realm_icon, etc. are not guaranteed to appear in the response.
    # * If they do, that means the server URL has only one realm on it
    # * If they don't, the server has multiple realms, and it's not clear which is
    #   the requested realm, so we can't send back these data.
```

As far as that's accurate, it'd be great for that info to propagate to the [`/server_settings` doc](https://zulip.com/api/get-server-settings), which currently doesn't say anything about those properties being missing. Reading code, if `realm_name` is missing, mobile will currently crash on the auth screen (the screen where you choose to auth with email/password, with Google, etc.), with an `Invariant Violation` error that says "ZulipText: `text` or `children` should be non-nullish". I think that's what's going on with [this Sentry issue](https://sentry.io/organizations/zulip/issues/3032804479/events/96dc6d89822f494999d463a4f8dcc300/?environment=production&project=191284) (link only works for those with access), looking at the stack trace there. (We also expect to see that error message in unrelated situations; it appears when our types tell us we have a string to render but the string is missing.)

I suppose we can have mobile recognize a missing `realm_name`, etc., as meaning "it's not clear which is the requested realm". Then, we'll want to know how we can be clearer which is the requested realm—the answer to that should also appear in the doc, I think. :smile:

## MessagesBase OpenAPI schema

*2022-03-09 to 2022-03-11 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/MessagesBase.20OpenAPI.20schema/with/1341539)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-03-09 17:18 UTC

With the message `edit_history` migration (#21309) last week, we added it as a property of the `MessagesBase` schema in the OpenAPI. As I'm working on a small refactor of that schema for #20576, I am wondering if we don't want that included in the documentation for the `/get-events`[ message event](https://chat.zulip.org/api/get-events#message).

As I understand it, the message event is for new messages and like `last_edit_timestamp`, will not be returned unless the message has been edited / moved, which is basically impossible if it's a brand new message event being sent from the server. And therefore, neither `edit_history` or `last_edit_timestamp` should be listed in the message object fields for that event.

Alternatively, we could have both the `edit_history` and `last_edit_timestamp` in the documentation for the event, but clearly state that it's not present if a message has never been edited. This is currently in the description for `edit_history`, but I'm thinking if we intend to keep this structure, then we should have the two fields in the base schema.

I lean towards the first option even though it will mean maybe having both a `NewMessagesBase` schema that's used directly by the event and a `MessagesBase` schema that builds off the other schema but adds in those history fields potentially present in existing messages, but feel like it would be good to get some consensus from folks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-09 19:40 UTC

I think from an API standpoint we should allow it to be possible for a new message to have edit history. There's a few reasons:
* It provides flexibility for potential features we may not have yet imagined where that might be useful.
* It provides the opportunity for the server=>clients event system to, should it choose to as an optimization, squash a "new message" event with an "edit message content" event if a client is disconnected from its event queue for an extended time. I don't think it's super likely we'll use this, but it seems like a fine reason to prefer one model over another for this detail.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-09 19:41 UTC

From a client perspective, it's also cleanest if the format is as identical as possible for a message fetched from any of our common APIs for getting them.

**Greg Price** · 2022-03-09 21:53 UTC

I agree with all of Tim's points.

There are a few existing differences between what a message object looks like in different parts of the API (notably, in get-messages it has a `flags` property, while the message in a `message` event has no `flags` property and instead the event itself has a `flags` property). From a client perspective, those are an annoying wart that adds complexity. I'd be glad to see them reconciled someday, and would like to not add more such differences.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-09 22:11 UTC

I suspect it wouldn't be hard to move the `flags` property from the event to the message object (well, duplicate for backwards-compatibility), since we're already doing custom per-user splicing; the cost is likely to just be some extra object copy operations in Python.  So we could reasonably file an issue for doing that.

Thanks for the feedback and thought processes / context behind it! It's hard sometimes to know when the small differences in the API are intentional and not.

This will simplify my API documentation updates for #20576 to be directly related to that update.

**Greg Price** · 2022-04-02 00:20 UTC

We have some existing notes on the results of that reverse-engineering, in `src/api/modelTypes.js`. Here they are:
```js
/**
 * The data encoded in a submessage to make the message a widget.
 *
 * Note that future server versions might introduce new types of widgets, so
 * `widget_type` could be a value not included here.  But when it is one of
 * these values, the rest of the object will follow this type.
 */
// Ideally we'd be able to express both the known and the unknown widget
// types: we'd have another branch of this union which looked like
//   | {| +widget_type: (string *other than* those above), +extra_data?: { ... } |}
// But there doesn't seem to be a way to express that in Flow.
export type WidgetData =
  | {|
      +widget_type: 'poll',
      +extra_data?: {| +question?: string, +options?: $ReadOnlyArray<string> |},
    |}
  // We can write these down more specifically when we implement these widgets.
  | {| +widget_type: 'todo', +extra_data?: { ... } |}
  | {| +widget_type: 'zform', +extra_data?: { ... } |};

/**
 * The data encoded in a submessage that acts on a widget.
 *
 * The interpretation of this data, including the meaning of the `type`
 * field, is specific to each widget type.
 *
 * We delegate actually processing these to shared code, so we don't specify
 * the details further.
 */
export type WidgetEventData = { +type: string, ... };

/**
 * The data encoded in a `Submessage`.
 *
 * For widgets (the only existing use of submessages), the submessages array
 * consists of:
 *  * One submessage with `WidgetData`; then
 *  * Zero or more submessages with `WidgetEventData`.
 */
export type SubmessageData = WidgetData | WidgetEventData;

/**
 * Submessages are items containing extra data that can be added to a
 * message. Despite what their name might suggest, they are not a subtype
 * of the `Message` type, nor do they share almost any fields with it.
 *
 * Submessages are used by Widgets:
 * https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/widgets.html
 *
 * Normally a message contains an empty array of these. We differentiate
 * between a normal message and a widget by the length of `submessages`
 * array property. Widgets will have 1 or more submessages.
 */
export type Submessage = $ReadOnly<{|
  id: number,
  message_id: number,
  sender_id: UserId,
  msg_type: 'widget', // only this type is currently available

  /** A `SubmessageData` object, JSON-encoded. */
  content: string,
|}>;
```

`.submessages` on message objects is documented to be `(string)[]`, e.g., in [`message` events](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#message). That can't be right; our type is

```js
  /** Servers <1.9.0 omit this; when omitted, equivalent to empty array. */
  // TODO(server-1.9): Make required.
  submessages?: $ReadOnlyArray<Submessage>,
```

and `Submessage` is

```js
/**
 * Submessages are items containing extra data that can be added to a
 * message. Despite what their name might suggest, they are not a subtype
 * of the `Message` type, nor do they share almost any fields with it.
 *
 * Submessages are used by Widgets:
 * https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/widgets.html
 *
 * Normally a message contains an empty array of these. We differentiate
 * between a normal message and a widget by the length of `submessages`
 * array property. Widgets will have 1 or more submessages.
 */
export type Submessage = $ReadOnly<{|
  id: number,
  message_id: number,

**Chris Bobbe** · 2022-06-07 02:28 UTC

````spoiler our SubmessageData type

```js
/**
 * The data encoded in a submessage to make the message a widget.
 *
 * Note that future server versions might introduce new types of widgets, so
 * `widget_type` could be a value not included here.  But when it is one of
 * these values, the rest of the object will follow this type.
 */
// Ideally we'd be able to express both the known and the unknown widget
// types: we'd have another branch of this union which looked like
//   | {| +widget_type: (string *other than* those above), +extra_data?: { ... } |}
// But there doesn't seem to be a way to express that in Flow.
export type WidgetData =
  | {|
      +widget_type: 'poll',
      +extra_data?: {| +question?: string, +options?: $ReadOnlyArray<string> |},
    |}
  // We can write these down more specifically when we implement these widgets.
  | {| +widget_type: 'todo', +extra_data?: { ... } |}
  | {| +widget_type: 'zform', +extra_data?: { ... } |};

/**
 * The data encoded in a submessage that acts on a widget.
 *
 * The interpretation of this data, including the meaning of the `type`
 * field, is specific to each widget type.
 *
 * We delegate actually processing these to shared code, so we don't specify
 * the details further.
 */
export type WidgetEventData = { +type: string, ... };

/**
 * The data encoded in a `Submessage`.
 *
 * For widgets (the only existing use of submessages), the submessages array
 * consists of:
 *  * One submessage with `WidgetData`; then
 *  * Zero or more submessages with `WidgetEventData`.
 */
export type SubmessageData = WidgetData | WidgetEventData;
```

````

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-22 00:52 UTC

Nope, that's not correct. Here's how that gets post-processed:
```
def post_process_state(                                                                                  
...
    if "raw_users" in ret:                                                                               
        user_dicts = list(ret["raw_users"].values())                                                     
        user_dicts = sorted(user_dicts, key=lambda x: x["user_id"])                                      
                                                                                                         
        ret["realm_users"] = [d for d in user_dicts if d["is_active"]]                                   
        ret["realm_non_active_users"] = [d for d in user_dicts if not d["is_active"]]                    
                                                                                                         
        """                                                                                              
        Be aware that we do intentional aliasing in the below code.                                      
        We can now safely remove the `is_active` field from all the                                      
        dicts that got partitioned into the two lists above.                                             
                                                                                                         
        We remove the field because it's already implied, and sending                                    
        it to clients makes clients prone to bugs where they "trust"                                     
        the field but don't actually update in live updates.  It also                                    
        wastes bandwidth.                                                                                
        """                                                                                              
        for d in user_dicts:                                                                             
            d.pop("is_active")                                                                           
                                                                                                         
        del ret["raw_users"]                                                                             
```

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:08 UTC

Those conditions on the client name seems like rather a hack. It's possible that one reason this part of the API isn't documented is that when one of us has looked at it to contemplate writing it down in docs, we've had the feeling that it should be revised into a better API instead.

(E.g., have the client pass another parameter that explicitly says it wants a particular flavor of mirror-user creation.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:10 UTC

So for your use case, if you want to get things going without needing any changes to the Zulip server code, it looks like you'll have to pick one of those flavors of mirror-user creation (probably Jabber or IRC -- Zephyr mirroring comes with extra specialness) where its behavior is close enough to what you want.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:16 UTC

As I understand your desired behavior, what you *really* want wouldn't involve any of this mirror-user creation at all. Those are really designed for situations where there's some other existing chat system that users are in, and a subset of the users are using Zulip while communicating with people who are using the other chat system and aren't Zulip users.

In particular, new users may show up at any time in the other chat system -- the first time Zulip learns about them is by the mirror receiving a message they sent, and wanting to propagate that message to Zulip. The mirror therefore handles that by creating user accounts in a special "mirror user" state. The corresponding humans may or may not later show up to Zulip themselves; if they do, using the same email address that's associated with their account in the external chat system, then they gain control of the account that their old messages are already attributed to.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:18 UTC

In your use case AIUI, by contrast, everyone has a Zulip account -- as new users enter the system, you'll make Zulip accounts for them up front. So the mirror should never have to create new user accounts. That also gets rid of all, I think, of the special logic where the Zulip server needs to know whether it's an IRC mirror or a Jabber mirror or whatever; the only thing the bot should need to do is say what users it's talking about. (And have the `can_forge_sender` permission, to be allowed to do that.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:26 UTC

I think that model makes a lot of sense, and would be good for the server code to support directly. If you're up for doing some patching of the Zulip server to support it (see docs for [tips on managing that operationally](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/upgrade-or-modify.html#making-changes)), I think the easiest way to get it working would probably be to make up one more `client.name` value to go alongside `irc_mirror` and `jabber_mirror` and the rest, and add a condition for it in `create_mirrored_message_users` as well as add it to that `if client.name in […]` list in `send_message_backend`.

In that condition, you'd just look up each of the users, in the realm that `user_profile` (i.e. the bot) belongs to, and check that they all exist there; if not, throw, and if they do, return, without calling `create_mirror_user_if_needed`.

This code could use some further refactoring beyond that, and some rework of the API, but that should be enough to get things working and reasonably clean.

(@Tim Abbott might have other suggestions when he's back next week from vacation.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:27 UTC

If you do go that path, I expect we'd be very interested in taking a PR to get that support upstream for everyone.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 05:29 UTC

If not, though, that's perfectly understandable. Take a look into the existing behavior with the client names `irc_mirror` and `jabber_mirror`; I expect you'll find that one or both of them will work well enough.

## realm settings names

*2022-06-24 to 2022-07-13 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/realm.20settings.20names/with/1396247)*

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:19 UTC

One thing I notice while reading #22291 (forking from [this thread](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/audit.20for.20change.20entries.20vs.2E.20central.20changelog/near/1395606)) -- a fact about our existing API changelog (and other parts of the API docs), not new with this change -- is that we aren't consistent about how to refer to realm settings.

To a large extent this is downstream of the unfortunate API design choice we have where most realm settings have two names, like `foo` and `realm_foo`. The `realm_foo` name appears in the /register response, and the unprefixed `foo` appears in events as described at https://zulip.com/api/get-events#realm-update_dict .

So then when referring to these settings in the API docs, in particular in the changelog, we typically use just one of those names. And we aren't consistent about which one we use.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:26 UTC

E.g. in the changelog, we say

> POST /register: Added realm_community_topic_editing_limit_seconds to the response

with the prefixed name, or

> POST /register: Added realm_giphy_rating and giphy_rating_options fields.

with the prefixed name for a realm setting (and the unprefixed name would be extremely confusing juxtaposed with another field that isn't a realm setting and has no prefixed name), but also

but also

> POST /register: Added a new wildcard_mention_policy setting for controlling who can use wildcard mentions in large streams.

or

> POST /register, GET /events, PATCH /realm: Added realm setting want_advertise_in_communities_directory for organizations to give permission to be advertised in the Zulip communities directory.

with the unprefixed name.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-24 20:30 UTC

I think I'm pretty happy with the style in that last example (which is also the most recent, from FL 129). Including formatting:

> `POST /register`, `GET /events`, `PATCH /realm`: Added realm setting `want_advertise_in_communities_directory` for organizations to give permission to be advertised in the Zulip communities directory.

where the first two endpoint references are links, and the third isn't because we don't have docs for setting realm settings (which is a gap I'm happy to leave at lowest priority for the short and medium term.)

So in particular:
* "realm setting `foo`", with that phrase "realm setting", to refer to the thing that's named `foo` in some parts of the API and `realm_foo` in others;
* in the API changelog, link to both /api/register-queue and /api/get-events, because the change appears in both those places.

## get-messages & num_* (num_before)

*2022-09-04 to 2024-05-13 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/get-messages.20.26.20num_.2A.20.28num_before.29/with/1430247)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2022-09-04 20:41 UTC

The documentation for `get-messages` appears inconsistent with the implementation, in regard to the `num_*` parameters (tested with `newest` so far).

Reading https://zulip.com/api/get-messages#parameters it indicates "newest" calculates the anchor (I assume a message id, as if passed in), and separately that the `num_*` values are the number *less than* or *greater than* the anchor id.

Therefore I would expect the following to return one message in a narrow:
`{"anchor": "newest", "num_before": 0, "num_after": 0, "narrow": x}`
That is, unless the narrow is empty, of course - and I can validate that is not the case in manual testing with some `x`  by increasing `num_before`.

However, the above gives me zero messages for a finite narrow, and testing with `"num_before": 1` gives me `1` message. That later approach is taken in the python-zulip-api helper for `move_topic` which calls `get_messages` here: https://github.com/zulip/python-zulip-api/blob/main/zulip/zulip/__init__.py#L1710 to acquire a message id for moving an entire topic.

I've not tested this more generally including with `oldest` and `first_unread`, or for that matter explicitly with a specific anchor message id, but there certainly seems an inconsistency here to fix in the documentation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:27 UTC

Interesting. This block of code in the implementation seems relevant:

``` python
# The semantics of our flags are as follows:                   
#                                                              
# num_after = number of rows < anchor                          
# num_after = number of rows > anchor                          
#                                                              
# But we also want the row where id == anchor (if it exists),  
# and we don't want to union up to 3 queries.  So in some cases
# we do things like `after_limit = num_after + 1` to grab the  
# anchor row in the "after" query.                             
#                                                              
# Note that in some cases, if the anchor row isn't found, we   
# actually may fetch an extra row at one of the extremes.      
if need_both_sides:                                            
    before_anchor = anchor - 1                                 
    after_anchor = max(anchor, first_visible_message_id)       
    before_limit = num_before                                  
    after_limit = num_after + 1                                
elif need_before_query:                                        
    before_anchor = anchor                                     
    before_limit = num_before                                  
    if not anchored_to_right:                                  
        before_limit += 1                                      
elif need_after_query:                                         
    after_anchor = max(anchor, first_visible_message_id)       
    after_limit = num_after + 1                                
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:28 UTC

Ahh; `anchored_to_right` corresponds to the `newest` case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:35 UTC

I suspect this is just a bug -- that the `not anchored_to_right` check there is wrong. 

For context, I believe that logic was written when that condition only happened when a client had manually passed an impossibly high anchor message ID like 10000000000 (see, for example, bd95b37d67532bed1c8951154c5cfe026199092d).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:36 UTC

And then in 05108760f68dc97079ebf1e6747defee326feb8b, we added support for the special "newest" string as a replacement for that ... but didn't change the semantics.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:41 UTC

In other words, what we're currently doing is translating "oldest" => 0 and "newest" => LARGER_THAN_MAX_MESSAGE_ID internally, such that the anchor ID used for the internal database query will never be a message ... but then failing to do the `before_limit + 1` logic in the "newest" case even those we do the equivalent `after_limit + 1` in the other case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:41 UTC

Looking at the history, I think that `not anchored_to_right` may be an erroneous refactor of when previously that wasn't an `elif` clause, or something like it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:42 UTC

So I think the thing to do is try this change and then write some tests for the corner cases that it might impact if there aren't any and see if the test changes confirm the reasoning above; it's possible I'm missing some other corner case.

```
diff --git a/zerver/views/message_fetch.py b/zerver/views/message_fetch.py
index 08e64cecd2..7f8192a605 100644
--- a/zerver/views/message_fetch.py
+++ b/zerver/views/message_fetch.py
@@ -1213,8 +1213,7 @@ def limit_query_to_range(
     elif need_before_query:
         before_anchor = anchor
         before_limit = num_before
-        if not anchored_to_right:
-            before_limit += 1
+        before_limit += 1
     elif need_after_query:
         after_anchor = max(anchor, first_visible_message_id)
         after_limit = num_after + 1
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:43 UTC

It appears all our tests pass if I apply that change, so I think this is indeed a corner case that is missing in `test_message_fetch.py`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-06 19:45 UTC

@Lauryn Menard would you be up for picking this up from here? 

One thing I'm not sure about is how to handle this detail in the API documentation; I suppose we could have a **Changes** note that before feature level X, if the "newest" parameter was used with `num_after=0`, a bug resulted in the response incorrectly containing 1 fewer message than it should, if indeed that proves to be the impact?

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-06 21:25 UTC

In this instance I think the actual behavior is somewhat cleaner than the documented behavior, and so ideally I think we'd fix the docs to match the code rather than vice versa. But either way would be fine.

Conceptually, I want the special anchors we call `newest` and `oldest` to have the meanings $$ \infty $$ and $$ -\infty $$, respectively -- they mean the very end and beginning of the message stream, beyond any messages that actually exist.

In particular, that semantics means that if I want the 100 latest messages, the number I pass (as `num_before`) is 100 -- no fiddling with off-by-ones is needed. If I want one message, I pass the number 1.

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-06 21:30 UTC

I think this can be done by just taking how the doc already describes `anchor` -- it's a "message ID", not a message -- and extending that to where it describes the special values.

So instead of
>  *`newest`: The most recent message.
> * `oldest`: The oldest message.

it'd be
> * `newest`: An ID newer than all actual messages.
> * `oldest`: An ID older than all actual messages.

So then `'anchor': 'newest'` and `'num_before': 10` would mean you get 10 "messages with IDs less than the anchor", which just means the 10 very latest messages.

*2022-09-12 to 2026-02-17 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/Need.20to.20update.20the.20API.20authentication.20section/with/1433928)*

**Ron Bertino** · 2022-09-12 00:18 UTC

The current documentation explains how to [get your API key](https://zulip.com/api/api-keys) for the bot, or a personal API key.
This part is fine.

If you then proceed to any of the documentation for the endpoints, such as [getting a user by email](https://zulip.com/api/get-user-by-email), and you then check out the usage example for curl, you'll see this:
```
curl -sSX GET -G https://yourZulipDomain.zulipchat.com/api/v1/users/iago@zulip.com \
    -u BOT_EMAIL_ADDRESS:BOT_API_KEY
```

Almost every user is going to assume that the above implies that they should be using a header with a key of BOT_EMAIL_ADDRESS and a value of the bot's API key.
That does not work.

After searching through this community, I found a reference to this issue and a [clear explanation was provided](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/127-integrations/topic/Post.20request.20from.20client.20side.20form/near/1261944).
You have to use HTTP basic authentication, providing the bot's email as the username and the bot's API key as the password.

I would be useful to add this information to the standard docs.

## User data clarifications

*2022-09-16 to 2022-10-14 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/User.20data.20clarifications/with/1436621)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2022-09-16 06:40 UTC

I was looking at improving ZT user handling, and some of the fixture data that we use, and so I was looking at the types/keys. Not all of this is something ZT will be addressing soon, but after looking at API documentation and limited testing, maybe someone could clarify these points before I dig in further:
- The `cross_realm_bots` appear to have a `delivery_email` available without my needing to be an admin. I understand that's maybe a special case and likely doesn't expose any private data or access, but it's confusing in that they don't appear to obey that general rule in the docs.
- Are `cross_realm_bots` always 'generic bots', or is that really somewhat of a filler field, with `is_system_bot` being an extra category beyond the numbered set (1,2,3,4) for output? 
- `is_active` only appears to be present on `cross_realm_bots` compared to other bots. Is that another quirk with those bots? I'm not that familiar with inactive/deactivated status generally, but `realm_non_active_users` appears to exist too - is it a subset of `realm_users`, which is why we have `is_active` generally?
- `timezone` appears to be present in bot data from the server, but always (?) empty. Is that a given right now, much like not bots not having any presence details?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-09-16 12:14 UTC

Let me try to respond on the points i have an idea about:

> The `cross_realm_bots` appear to have a `delivery_email` available without my needing to be an admin. I understand that's maybe a special case and likely doesn't expose any private data or access, but it's confusing in that they don't appear to obey that general rule in the docs.

Yeah, this doesn't expose any data, because those bots live in the system realm, are kind of hard-coded entities and are "public" to all users. Probably we should just be documenting this special-case behavior regarding `delivery_email` being present? I hope we can at some point push forward with just getting rid of the whole concept of cross-realm bots though, it would simplify things a lot.

- Are `cross_realm_bots` always 'generic bots', or is that really somewhat of a filler field, with `is_system_bot` being an extra category beyond the numbered set (1,2,3,4) for output? 

I believe `cross_realm_bots` and `is_system_bot` are the same thing. As said above, these bots live in `zulipinternal` realm and are hard-coded, the server code uses them for sending messages sometimes. Like `Welcome Bot` and its initial messages to user. `Notification bot` for various things, `Email gateway bot` which sends message coming from the incoming email integration etc.

>  `is_active` only appears to be present on `cross_realm_bots` compared to other bots. 

Hmm, not quite sure but my guess would be on this being just a quirk of how user info dicts are created, and cross-realm bot accounts going through the same codepath as human users, while other bots do not? I'm more suprised by `is_active` being absent for other bots i guess :thinking: 


> `realm_non_active_users` appears to exist too - is it a subset of `realm_users`, which is why we have `is_active` generally?

Seems  correct, looking at the code here:
```
    if "raw_users" in ret:
        user_dicts = list(ret["raw_users"].values())
        user_dicts = sorted(user_dicts, key=lambda x: x["user_id"])

        ret["realm_users"] = [d for d in user_dicts if d["is_active"]]
        ret["realm_non_active_users"] = [d for d in user_dicts if not d["is_active"]]
```

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 16:39 UTC

Good questions. This is a part of the API that has some confusing quirks in it.

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> - … I'm not that familiar with inactive/deactivated status generally, but `realm_non_active_users` appears to exist too - is it a subset of `realm_users`, which is why we have `is_active` generally?

Not a subset -- the name `realm_users` is misleading. In fact `realm_users` has only the users that are not deactivated, while `realm_non_active_users` has the users that are deactivated. (And both exclude cross-realm bots.)

So to get a complete list of users, you combine those two lists plus `cross_realm_bots`. And perhaps fill in an `is_active` property based on which list you got the user from.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 16:40 UTC

That caveat on `realm_users` [is actually documented](https://zulip.com/api/register-queue). I hope we can clean up the actual API around it someday.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 16:51 UTC

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> - `timezone` appears to be present in bot data from the server, but always (?) empty. Is that a given right now, much like not bots not having any presence details?

Here's the notes we have on that property in mobile:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/2d1762709/src/api/modelTypes.js#L217
```js
// export type User = …
  // The ? is for future-proofing. Greg explains in 2020-02, at
  // https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/pull/3789#discussion_r378554698 ,
  // that both human and bot Users will likely end up having a missing
  // timezone instead of an empty string.
  +timezone?: string,

// export type CrossRealmBot = …
  // The ? is for future-proofing.  For bots it's always '':
  //   https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/pull/3789#issuecomment-581218576
  // so a future version may omit it to reduce payload sizes.  See comment
  // on the same field in User.
  +timezone?: string,
```

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 16:54 UTC

One thing we should document, and doesn't seem to be in the existing docs, is that `timezone` may be the empty string and that that means there's no information on the user's timezone.

(That's based on the two GitHub comments linked from those notes.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 16:55 UTC

And yeah, the current behavior is that for bots (both cross-realm and otherwise) it's always present and is the empty string, because we don't have a timezone for bots.

The future-proof thing for a client is probably to expect that in the future it may be omitted when there's no information there, instead of `timezone: ''`.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 17:00 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)
> > `is_active` only appears to be present on `cross_realm_bots` compared to other bots. Hmm, not quite sure but my guess would be on this being just a quirk of how user info dicts are created, and cross-realm bot accounts going through the same codepath as human users, while other bots do not? I'm mo …

I think what's happening here is:
* `is_active` is omitted in the elements of `realm_users` and `realm_non_active_users`.
* But it's present in `cross_realm_bots`, just as it is in contexts like /api/get-user .

So it's not so much about cross-realm bots vs. other bots, as cross-realm bots vs. all other users; and really it's due to that quirk that the users in the /api/register-queue response are spread across three different lists.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-14 17:02 UTC

Oh also, there's an error in the documentation (perhaps one that's annoying to fix due to how we share descriptions between different parts of the API):
* In /api/register-queue, `is_active` appears in the list of properties for the elements of `realm_users` and `realm_non_active_users`. But in fact, as the description at the top of each of those explains, `is_active` doesn't appear in those objects.

* [Clarifying that](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/User.20data.20clarifications/near/1449862) `timezone` may be the empty string, and what it means if it is.
* Perhaps trying to do something to further clarify [the relationship between `realm_users` and `realm_non_active_users`](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/User.20data.20clarifications/near/1449856). ## security scheme validation/testing

*2022-09-16 to 2022-09-16 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/security.20scheme.20validation.2Ftesting/with/1436711)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-09-16 16:33 UTC

I looked at #22938, which fixes a capitalization typo in OpenAPI documentation, and why it's failing tests.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-09-16 16:33 UTC

It seems like we haven't actually been validating the security scheme defined in `zulip.yaml` correctly since the update from OpenAPI 2.0 to 3.0.1 ([relevant commit](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/f1935f4c735d75fbf2db84e99d8b1af6a950eb99)) due to said capitalization error.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-09-16 16:33 UTC

And when we fix that, the 3rd party openapi_core validation we're using in doesn't realize the Django authorization header we set for the test's request (`"HTTP_AUTHORIZATION"`) is the authorization header. It's looking for `"Authorization"` to compare against the security scheme.

We can fix that in `validate_request` in `openapi.py`.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-09-16 16:33 UTC

But where I'm running into an issue in that we call `validate_api_response_openapi` in the various `client_` functions (e.g., `client_post`). But those only have the request authorization header set for the test if they are called through their `api` counterparts (e.g., `api_post`).

I think it would be helpful context for me to know why we have both the `client_` and `api_` functions in the test suite.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-09-16 16:34 UTC

Let me know if I can clarify anything above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:50 UTC

@Lauryn Menard yeah, I can explain that detail.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:51 UTC

The `api_` functions do API authentication: Passing an email/api-key pair via HTTP basic authentication.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:51 UTC

In contrast, the `client_` functions use the current browser session, aka you need to call `self.login()` first.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:52 UTC

The `api_` are generally nicer to use, in that doing an API request as user X via those functions works the same whether or not the caller logged in as a different user or whatever.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:53 UTC

(One generally doesn't want to write a test helper that calls `self.login`, since it would create a confusing side effect when reading the code of the caller)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:54 UTC

So the tricky thing here is likely that Zulip's API with the `/api/v1/` URLs only allows API authentication, but we're trying to use the validator to also verify the requests/responses for the parallel `/json/` URLs used by browsers, which we don't really intend to recommend for end users and thus document.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 18:55 UTC

(As a sidenote, we should probably reorganize and add docstrings for the `api_` helpers so this isn't a question one needs to ask)


## OpenAPI 3.1

*2022-10-08 to 2022-10-13 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/OpenAPI.203.2E1/with/1446558)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-10-08 01:28 UTC

With today’s openapi-core upgrade (#23160), I think we’re finally able to upgrade our schema to OpenAPI 3.1. There are a bunch of OpenAPI 3.1 features we’ve been itching to use, such as replacing the `nullable` boolean with a real `null` type, and replacing `additionalProperties` with [`unevaluatedProperties`](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/object.html#unevaluated-properties) to avoid the need for separate `Foo` and `FooBase` schemas whenever we want to use inheritance.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-12 22:52 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> replacing `additionalProperties` with [`unevaluatedProperties`](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/object.html#unevaluated-properties) to avoid the need for separate `Foo` and `FooBase` schemas whenever we want to use inheritance.

That sounds like a very nice improvement!

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-13 00:14 UTC

Yeah, those sound great. More generally I've been pretty pleased with new OpenAPI versions actually fixing important limitations in the language.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-10-13 06:04 UTC

The news here isn’t OpenAPI 3.1 (released 2021-02-18), it’s that openapi-core supports it now.

def normalize_body(body: str) -> str:
    body = body.rstrip().lstrip("\n")
    if len(body) == 0:
        raise JsonableError(_("Message must not be empty"))
    if "\x00" in body:
        raise JsonableError(_("Message must not contain null bytes"))
    return truncate_content(body, settings.MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH, "\n[message truncated]")
```

This code path is the `internal_send_message` code path primarily intended for use in the email gateway.

So the 4000 here was I think intentionally different from 10000; the intent was I think "If this email that came into the email gateway was too long, then truncate it at some smaller size so you don't end up with a giant truncated email going through." I think it's very reasonable to try removing that feature and see if there's an apparent downside. The 4000 rule was set before we introduced `talon` for stripping footers from emails, and also probably before we added the condensing of very tall messages in the web app's message feed.

So I think it's reasonable to remove it as a misfeature, but wanted to provide that context.

I don't write a lot of Java, but it's pretty hard to believe that nobody's made a JSON library for Java that can handle an array of strings in a nice way.

And indeed, here's [example code](https://github.com/google/gson/blob/master/UserGuide.md#array-examples) I found in a couple minutes' googling:
```java
Gson gson = new Gson();
String[] strings = {"abc", "def", "ghi"};
gson.toJson(strings);  // ==> ["abc", "def", "ghi"]
```

If you aren't currently using a JSON implementation that gets you anything reasonably nice like that, maybe you should be using Gson. Or another good one — probably it's not the only one with a reasonable interface like that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-23 02:20 UTC

As written, neither of those are valid requests for the Zulip API. A valid request is formatted as either `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`:

```
DELETE /api/v1/users/me/subscriptions HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:9991
Authorization: Basic YWFyb25AenVsaXAuY29tOnBhc3N3b3Jk
Content-Length: 49
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

subscriptions=%5B%22Verona%22%2C+%22Denmark%22%5D
```

or `multipart/form-data`:

```
DELETE /api/v1/users/me/subscriptions HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:9991
Authorization: Basic YWFyb25AenVsaXAuY29tOnBhc3N3b3Jk
Content-Length: 169
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=------------------------86b88971a074c58f

--------------------------86b88971a074c58f
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="subscriptions"

["Verona", "Denmark"]
--------------------------86b88971a074c58f--
```

These formats are fundamentally only capable of encoding values that are (byte)strings. Some other services allow an entire request to be formatted as `application/json`, but we do not (except for certain webhook requests where the format is defined by the sender).

Perhaps your HTTP client library is translating your request to `application/x-www-form-encoded` or `multipart/form-data`, and it’s using a non-JSON translation for array values by default.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-18 22:20 UTC

(replying to Lauryn Menard)
> Regarding that ... I've noticed that the not-real `email` is often referred to as "Zulip display email" and once as "Zulip API email" in the description of `user` objects. I think it would be good to land on a phrasing / terminology that feels clear that we use in this case. Based on the general usa …

Yeah, good thought.

I think I actually prefer the term "Zulip API email". It feels clearer to me for a couple of reasons:
* Saying "display email" sounds like it's specifying something about what a UI will do — what it will display. But that's generally not in scope for API docs. The API docs sometimes offer important *advice* on what a UI should do, but it never makes sense for them to just make assumptions about what a UI will do, because UIs will differ.
* In particular, when a UI is showing a user's email, the `delivery_email` is the one it will usually prefer to display. When the `email` and `delivery_email` are two different strings, that means the `email` is a synthetic fake email address that basically exists for internal technical reasons. For any UI that's aimed at normal users, that means that one wants to display either the delivery email or no email at all, and that's the approach that web and mobile (at least) have moved to.

  So that means that the most natural reading of the phrase "Zulip display email" would probably be `delivery_email`, not `email`.
* Conversely, "Zulip API email" feels like it pretty well captures what the `email` field means: it's the "email" that exists for identifying the user in parts of the Zulip API.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-18 22:24 UTC

(replying to Lauryn Menard)
> And just to check/confirm, since adding the user level control for the email visibility, a bot's email should always be the `delivery_email`, correct?

Disabling cycling in PM while editing ( #T1280 ) ), I noticed that the web app doesn't send typing notifications to recipients while editing an already sent message. I think that is the expected behavior as well because I think typing indicators are usually associated with incoming messages.

But could not find this information in the [docs](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/typing-indicators.html)(probably needs a bit of addition). Also, the mobile app sends typing notifications to recipients while editing an already sent message. **Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-15 16:22 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-15 16:22 UTC

**Alya Abbott** · 2023-05-15 16:28 UTC

#**design>typing notifications for editing?**

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-15 18:58 UTC

I think that docs page does already specify this. Since you didn't take that from the page, though, it'd probably be good to make it more explicit.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-15 18:58 UTC

The page says at the outset:
> Typing indicators are status messages that tell you when another user is composing a message to you. 

And then in the more spec-like details, it says:
> When a “writing user” starts to compose a message, the client app sends a request […]

So both are about when a user is "composing" a message — which describes when they're preparing one to send, and wouldn't be a normal term to describe editing a message.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-15 19:02 UTC

(replying to Subhasish-Behera)
> Also, the mobile app sends typing notifications to recipients while editing an already sent message.

Interesting, thanks. That's probably best seen as a bug.

In general the edit-message UI in the mobile app is somewhat unloved; as you noted, the UX for it is borrowed from composing a message (and rather awkwardly so), and the code to implement editing a message is likewise rather jammed into the code for composing. One consequence is that it's easy to accidentally pick up behaviors that compose has even when they aren't intended.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-23 19:14 UTC

(replying to Lauryn Menard)
> API changelog entry: Minor note here about the use of "attributes" here ... > `POST /register`: Added the `server_presence_ping_interval_seconds` and `server_presence_offline_threshold_seconds` attributes.

I tend to prefer "property" here.

There's no term for this in the JSON spec — it just says an object consists of "name/value pairs", so if one had to express this in pure JSON-spec terms you'd say something like "Added name/value pairs with names `server_presence_ping_interval_seconds` and `server_presence_offline_threshold_seconds`".

But JSON is after all based on JavaScript, and the JS term for these is "property". The [spec section describing objects](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-object-type) begins:
> An Object is logically a collection of properties.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-23 19:16 UTC

I think the reason the docs sometimes have "attribute" is that that's the corresponding Python term for the things an object has.

(Though it's not really a great fit here even in a Python-centric context, because these JSON properties don't map to Python attributes when deserialized — they map to Python key/value pairs, in a Python dict.)

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-23 19:17 UTC

I don't think "constant" is a good fit, because after all the reason they're there in the /api/register-queue response is that they're not necessarily constant. If they were truly constant, we could just specify them in the API docs.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-23 19:17 UTC

What does the schema language that Zulip uses (I forget its name) use for key/value pairs?

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-23 19:18 UTC

Good question. OpenAPI is the name.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-23 19:37 UTC

I would consider "fields" as an alternative to "properties" or "attributes".  They are probably all easy enough to deduce from context, but none of them are quite perfect.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-23 23:32 UTC

```
$ git grep propert api_docs/ zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml | wc
    348    1377   25981
$ git grep attribut api_docs/ zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml | wc
     15     163    1595
$ git grep field api_docs/ zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml | wc
    324    2857   31478
$ git grep propert api_docs/ zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml  | grep -v properties: | grep -v property: | wc
     98     857   10499
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-23 23:34 UTC

I think `field` is what we use most often in prose we wrote -- as you can see in the last one, `properties` appears a bunch in the OpenAPI spec file.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-24 03:03 UTC

A lot of the matches for "field" are talking about custom profile fields.

Here's a count that excludes some of those:
```
$ git grep -n field api_docs/ zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml | grep -ve 'profile.field' -e '_field' -e 'field_' | wc -l
213
```
but when you look, a lot of those are still about custom profile fields: "field type 7", "date-based fields", "whether to display the field in a small/summary section", and so on.

I think it's still more than the uses of "property", but it's about 2:1 and not 3:1.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-24 03:09 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> `properties` appears a bunch in the OpenAPI spec file.

And from looking at where this appears, I think we have an answer to @Steve Howell's question from above: OpenAPI says "property" for the name/value pairs in a JSON object.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 03:10 UTC

I think I lean toward "properties" here, especially in light of the OpenAPI usage.  I think "fields" would also be fine.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-24 03:11 UTC

([The spec](https://swagger.io/specification/) also uses the term "field" a lot… but always, AFAICT, to refer to something that appears within an OpenAPI schema itself, never to refer to something that appears in the API the schema describes. That seems like probably a choice they've made specifically to avoid confusion between those two.)

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 03:12 UTC

Yeah, I think this is just a case where language is tough.  Fortunately, I don't think the stakes are super high here, as most folks will figure out stuff from context.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 03:21 UTC

Yeah, specifically to the `stream_id` parameter of /api/update-message. The term "parameter" is usefully more specific than the generic "property" or "field", in that it flags that this is something passed by the client to the server in its request.

There's also the fun fact that in our API, a request parameter isn't a JSON property at all — the parameters are not represented as a JSON object. Rather they're HTML form data, so encoded like `foo=3&bar=4`, with the values URL-encoded.

(That fun fact is one of the handful of notoriously underdocumented areas of our API. The one place you can learn it unambiguously, AFAIK, is from the "curl" tab on each usage example, and then looking up in the `curl` man page the `--data-urlencode` option we use there.)

## use of oneOf in schema

*2023-05-18 to 2023-05-19 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/use.20of.20oneOf.20in.20schema/with/1571989)*

**Brijmohan Siyag** · 2023-05-18 19:39 UTC

While I was writing Api docs for [Previewable URLs](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/Previewable.20URL.20Api), I used `oneOf` inside `allOf` than this happened that return values were from first schema of `oneOf` only.  This should include all other properties from `allOf`. 

After looking at other implementations I found that we are using description to mention if a property is optional. Is it what we are using in general or this is a bug in openapi rendering.

I found the function which is responsible for this.
```python
def get_openapi_return_values(endpoint: str, method: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    operation = openapi_spec.openapi()["paths"][endpoint][method.lower()]
    schema = operation["responses"]["200"]["content"]["application/json"]["schema"]
    # In cases where we have used oneOf, the schemas only differ in examples
    # So we can choose any.
    if "oneOf" in schema:
        schema = schema["oneOf"][0]
    return schema["properties"]
```

I did `git log` to see where the if statement for `oneOf` was introduced but there was only one log stating "python: Normalize quotes with Black.". 


Example - 
```yaml
/previewable:
  post:
    operationId: previewable
    summary: Endpoint to fetch data of a previewable URL.
    tags: ["messages"]
    description: |
      Returns data of a URL to preview.
    parameters:
      - name: url
        in: query
        description: |
          URL to preview.
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: string
            example: "https://www.github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/19710"
        required: true
    responses:
      "200":
        description: Success.
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              allOf:
                - type: object
                  properties:
                    platform:
                      type: string
                      description: |
                        Platform
                    type:
                      type: string
                      description: |
                        Type of issue
                      enum: [issue, pull_request]
                - oneOf:
                  - type: object
                    properties:
                      merged_at:
                        example: issue
                        type: string
                      draft:
                        example: issue
                        type: boolean
                  - type: object
                    properties:
                      state_reason:
                        type: string
                        example: "The issue was closed because it was a duplicate."
```

So this is rendering `merged_at` and `draft` in "Return values" but this should include `platform`, `type` atleast.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-24 16:25 UTC

OK. Here's hopefully a better attempt at describing the relationship between these and how it's changed:

Originally, the history entries (in message objects, and in /api/get-message-history) contained only the *old* state of things — not the new state. The idea was that you already know the very latest state, from the rest of the message object itself; and if you start with that and walk backward through the history entries, you can work out what the state was at each step. So showing the *new* state of things would just be redundant, because it's always information that you already have (either from a later history entry, or from the current state of the message.)

So there was `prev_stream` but no `stream`, and there was `prev_subject` but no `subject` (nor `topic`).

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-24 16:27 UTC

Then we decided that it was easier to consume the history if each history entry was self-contained. So we added `stream`; and rather than add `subject`, we combined that transition with migrating that name, so replaced `prev_subject` with `prev_topic` and added `topic`.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-25 16:44 UTC

If you're writing a client and you really are interested in just a particular old version of the server, then it's presumably one you have running, and so you can find the documentation at `/api/` on that server — `https://chat.example/api/`.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-25 16:48 UTC

API docs differ from server docs in that the audience is people writing clients, and someone writing a client is much more likely to be interested in supporting a whole range of versions than in supporting a specific old version.

That's why our approach to compatibility in the API docs has been to have the current version of the docs describe the behavior of all versions of the server going back to basically the point where we got serious about API docs. This is more work on the documentation side than just serving up old snapshots of the docs, but it saves a ton of work on the client side — realistically one would not be able to maintain a client reliably compatible with old server versions without it.

## documenting error responses

*2023-07-04 to 2024-06-26 · 50 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/documenting.20error.20responses/with/1603333)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-07-04 03:07 UTC

I wanted to ask do we prefer to document all type of error responses in the API documentation or not. I know we do not document all of them for many endpoints currently, but do we want to document all the new error responses.

I am asking this as I am working on #**issues>"@" in user group name** which results in a new error response for invalid user group names.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-04 03:21 UTC

Good question. I'm not sure we have an explicit consensus on this. My answer would be:

* For errors that have the generic `BAD_REQUEST` error code — which is most of our errors, which is fine — there's no need for specific documentation.

  After all, client code shouldn't be trying to inspect those errors anyway. There's no information there but the error message, and the error message is never suitable for client code to try to inspect: in particular it gets translated for the user's language, and the text might get tweaked at any time for user-facing clarity.

* If there are errors with a more specific error code, and we know of a use case for client code to want to inspect the specifics of the error, then it should get documented.

  There are very few examples of this. One is BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID on /api/get-events (see bottom of page) — that's in fact the one that motivated the error-code system in the first place, back in 2017.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-04 03:22 UTC

For an invalid name for a user group, I'd expect us to just give the generic BAD_REQUEST code, and a message that's informative for the user.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-04 03:22 UTC

(on attempting to create such a group, that is)

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-05 22:12 UTC

Yeah, when the error messages aren't in scope to be covered in the documentation, I wouldn't cover changes to them in "Changes" notes either.

We do document in the API changelog (and in "Changes" notes where applicable) some changes to things that aren't themselves documented. But that's for things like setting realm settings, or (taking the most recent example on /api/changelog right now) to `POST /export/realm` — where the thing is perfectly well in scope for documentation in principle, and we just haven't gotten around to documenting it. Error messages, by contrast, aren't part of the defined API at all, and a perfect version of our API docs still wouldn't document them.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-05 22:14 UTC

(replying to Sahil Batra)
> We had a check at database level previously not at API level, so it returned an error previously but not a 400 response.

Hmm, does that mean it'd return a 5xx response? In that case, that change is fixing a bug. :smile:

Typically we don't record bugfixes in the API changelog or in "Changes" notes. We only do so when there's reason to think clients might have been relying on the bug, or when there's something clients will want to do on older versions to work around the bug. Here I think clients should just ignore it, so there's no need to describe it in the API docs.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-07-06 07:27 UTC

> Hmm, does that mean it'd return a 5xx response?

Yes.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-07-06 07:28 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-28 20:13 UTC

In the context of validation, not documenting error response messages also helps us switch to [a different error handling mechanism](https://catt.rs/en/stable/validation.html#detailed-validation). Particularly, we might use exception groups  ([PEP 654](https://peps.python.org/pep-0654/)) to combine all validation errors together before putting them together in a single response.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-30 01:32 UTC

Error handling for validation failures is now implemented in #26365 in the commit of converters.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-08 20:56 UTC

So I actually am not particularly a fan of the API design approach that tries to find all the problems with your request and return them together; I prefer the model where the server rejects a request as soon as it finds the first validation failure; to me at least, doing so makes it a lot easier to write secure server code because you make clearer assumptions. And I don't think when writing an API client I've ever particularly liked getting 2 different validation exceptions combined together in some way.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 04:05 UTC

Huh, this is kind of wacky. I think `msg` doesn't make a lot of sense when there isn't an error to have an error message about.

I think I'd prefer to think of that as a legacy quirk, and either (a) not document it or (b) document it as deprecated. That way we reduce the risk of someone accidentally coming to depend on it, before we someday go and remove it.

So then it'd be something like:
* every response has `result`, of "error" or "success"
* when it's a success response, the rest is documented on the endpoint (except oh there's also a deprecated `"msg": ""`)
* when it's an error response, it also has
  * `msg`
  * `code`
  * possibly other keys depending on `code`
