> [This conversation](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/general/subject/mark.20all.20messages.20read/near/90307) might be of interest to people who are interested in Zulip terms/a Zulip glossary
This quoted message has a link of a different format that at least zulip-terminal doesn't understand, but the web app does. This seems to be a variant where we need to also accept `subject/` in the URL, as an alternative to `topic/`?

This was from late 2016, so pre-2.1.0 and *well* before feature levels, but older servers may have messages of this format - so this is a case where clients which want to support servers that *were* older but now even on `main` will need to support a very old format. I know we've discussed these multiple times, but are existing and older formats documented?

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-03 19:37 UTC

No, the narrow URLs are one of the remaining few areas that are unfortunately still in need of documentation.

And I agree, this is something where clients need to support old servers' behavior indefinitely.

Yeah we should document that `subject` is a deprecated alias for `topic`. I think I would not want us to start having new endpoints do something different — I'd prefer to hold off on that until we have a plan for migrating everything (or at least everything-but-a-few-exceptions) to support all JSON. Even then, it's probably better if new endpoints support both forms for as long as all the existing endpoints do.

The thing is that if any given client has to support talking to some endpoints in all-JSON form at the same time as other endpoints are in `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with our existing mixture of sometimes using JSON inside the values, that state is even messier than the status quo.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-10 02:00 UTC

Agreed. This feels like something that we can aim for while working on the `has_request_variables` migration. Particularly, `REQ` parameters that use `json_validator` (JSON-encoded query parameters for the clients) are some known blockers.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-10 02:07 UTC

Pydantic now has a [`Json` annotation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/usage/types/json/) for this, and we’ll need it for `GET` and `DELETE` requests regardless of what we do for `POST` and `PATCH`, so there isn’t anything to be gained by blocking these things on each other.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-16 19:45 UTC

While we use `json_validator=check_bool` for parameters that accepts booleans, the API documentation doesn't mention the fact that the boolean has to be valid JSON.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-16 19:48 UTC

Actually, it might be fine. [OpenAPI spec](https://swagger.io/docs/specification/data-models/data-types/#boolean) only allows `true` and `false` for the `boolean` type

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-16 21:55 UTC

My current workaround to the fact that the parameters are defined as `Json` but not in the OpenAPI spec is to exempt primitive types `int`, `bool` from doing the check on the content type.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-16 21:55 UTC

Perhaps once we migrate to a JSON-encoded request body, this workaround will no longer be needed.

- [[Bug]: Can’t validate integer/number/boolean from application/x-www-form-urlencoded request body #700](https://github.com/python-openapi/openapi-core/issues/700)

openapi: Loosen anchor parameter specification to string.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 22:35 UTC

Yeah. [#698](https://github.com/python-openapi/openapi-core/issues/698) seems like it’s going to be difficult though. The standard doesn’t seem to have anything to say about exactly how and where strings get cast to integers, and I’m not really sure what it *should* say.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 22:38 UTC

As a thought experiment, in a context where we’re allowed to auto-cast `"123"` to an integer, should it validate as `{"oneOf": [{"type": "integer"}, {"type": "string"}]}`? (Note here that `oneOf` means exactly one, as opposed to `anyOf` which means at least one.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 22:42 UTC

If we wanted to unconditionally force the integer interpretation, we could declare it JSON-encoded. But that’s not what we want for `anchor`, because the `newest`/`oldest`/`first_unread` values are not JSON-encoded.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 22:43 UTC

I think the correct conclusion is that this is a bad API.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-31 22:48 UTC

I certainly agree it'd be better if the request bodies were all JSON, instead of our mix of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with occasionally some values being in JSON.

In the world of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, though, I think the choice of having bare `first_unread` etc. to go along with numbers `123` is a pretty reasonable one. Certainly if I were looking at a URL and the query looked like `?anchor="first_unread"&…`, I'd think the quotes were a bit of a wart.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-31 22:49 UTC

If `oneOf` is supposed to mean exactly one, then that seems to force the answer to your thought experiment to be that it doesn't validate.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-31 22:52 UTC

From your issue description, our use case is `{"oneOf": [{"type": "string", "enum": ["newest", "oldest", "first_unread"]}, {"type": "integer"}]}`.

In the first branch of that, we really do mean the enum of those three values — not all strings in general. So on its face that doesn't seem to raise the same issue with an input like "123".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 22:58 UTC

`{"oneOf": [{"type": "integer"}, {"type": "string"}]}` lives entirely within the world of JSON schemas, where strings and numbers are disjoint, so it validates both the number `123` and the string `"123"`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 23:00 UTC

The data flow for the `x-www-form-urlencoded` world is supposed to be `x-www-form-urlencoded` string → JSON value → JSON schema validation. But it seems that any solution to this question with the properties we want for `anchor` has to break this flow.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 23:01 UTC

In some sense, even a simple `{"type": "integer"}` parameter breaks this flow—you have to peek inside the JSON schema to decide whether to cast the `x-www-form-urlencoded` string to a JSON integer.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-31 23:08 UTC

It’s probably reasonable to special-case `{"type": "integer"}` (and `number` and `boolean`), as openapi-core does, even though I can’t find any language in the standard that specifies that. However, from an objective standards point of view, I don’t see a reasonable way to specify that casting for anything more complicated, or a good case that it should be specified. We’ve basically made up our own encoding for a value that might or might not be an integer, so the only objective resolution would be to schematize it as a `string` that our code happens to parse in some custom way.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-31 23:34 UTC

Hmm I see, I hadn't absorbed that the `oneOf` and `"type": "integer"` and so on that appear in OpenAPI definitions are defined in terms of JSON schemas. I agree that makes it an awkward fit for describing this bit of the API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-01 21:06 UTC

I think ultimately we should try to avoid spending too much time on tweaking details of the existing encoding of this fairly rare class of parameters, if we can avoid it.

At least, I feel like at some point that might not be super distant, we're probably going to do an `/api/v2` that encodes all the parameters as a single JSON blob (whether we change the URLs or not), and this seems like the kind of detail that I'd rather not spend much time migrating individually vs. just including in such a migration.

> The user ID of the other participant in this non-group direct message conversation. Will be your own user ID for messages that you sent to only yourself.

> Old name for `other_user_id`. Clients should access this field in Zulip server versions that do not yet support `other_user_id`.

## avatar_url: Request specific size

*2023-09-07 to 2026-06-08 · 77 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/avatar_url.3A.20Request.20specific.20size/with/1636546)*

**Chris Bobbe** · 2023-09-07 22:42 UTC

When displaying an avatar image, clients are responsible for choosing the right URL for the image size they want. It would be helpful to document how clients should make that choice, for any given value of `avatar_url` on user objects (and I suppose message objects).

Here's how `zulip-mobile` does it. Parts of this logic grew from reverse engineering and various CZO threads:

- When `avatar_url` is `null`, we compute a Gravatar URL. (The method of doing that might be good to specify; I can elaborate on how zulip-mobile does it.) For the size, we follow [this Gravatar doc](https://en.gravatar.com/site/implement/images/#size) for how to adjust the URL.
- When `avatar_url` is missing, we use `<realm>/avatar/{userId}` if ≤100 pixels is desired, else `<realm>/avatar/{userId}/medium`. That "100" is a hard-coded constant that's meant to mimic the server's `DEFAULT_AVATAR_SIZE` constant.
- When `avatar_url` is a string starting with `https://secure.gravatar.com/`, we follow that Gravatar doc mentioned above.
- When `avatar_url` is some other string, we use it directly if ≤100 pixels is desired, else we replace the pattern `/(?:\.png)?$/` with '-medium.png'. (The same point about 100 / `DEFAULT_AVATAR_SIZE` applies.) We have a comment explaining the `?` in that pattern: the input string will end in ".png" for local uploads, and it will not for s3 uploads. Presumably we're correct to include ".png" in the "medium" variant for both backends, or we'd have heard complaints.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-30 18:44 UTC

They do. Probably we should actually do the small refactor to make it more formally two endpoints; we can use `int:` in the paths. Here's what we have for these avatar endpoints:

```
    # Avatars have the same constraint because their URLs are included                                  
    # in API data structures used by both the mobile and web clients.                                   
    rest_path(                                                                                          
        "avatar/<email_or_id>",                                                                         
        GET=(avatar, {"override_api_url_scheme", "allow_anonymous_user_web"}),                          
    ),                                                                                                  
    rest_path(                                                                                          
        "avatar/<email_or_id>/medium",                                                                  
        GET=(                                                                                           
            avatar_medium,                                                                              
            {"override_api_url_scheme", "allow_anonymous_user_web"},                                    
        ),                                                                                              
    ),                                                                                                  
```

And the similar endpoints for users, where we just place the `<int:user_id>` one first so that all requests in integer format go there:
```
rest_path(                                                                                   
    "users/<int:user_id>",                                                                   
    GET=get_members_backend,                                                                 
    PATCH=update_user_by_id_api,                                                             
    DELETE=deactivate_user_backend,                                                          
),                                                                                           
rest_path("users/<email>", GET=get_user_by_email, PATCH=update_user_by_email_api),           
```

So we can do that preparatory refactor.

@cache_with_key(user_profile_cache_key, timeout=3600 * 24 * 7)
def get_user(email: str, realm: "Realm") -> UserProfile:
    """Fetches the user by its visible-to-other users username (in the
    `email` field).  For use in API contexts; do not use in
    authentication/registration contexts as doing so will break
    authentication in organizations using
    EMAIL_ADDRESS_VISIBILITY_ADMINS.  In those code paths, use

        "realm__direct_message_initiator_group__named_user_group",
        "realm__direct_message_permission_group",

## mark-as-read events on stream unsubscribe

*2023-09-13 to 2023-09-13 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/mark-as-read.20events.20on.20stream.20unsubscribe/with/1639261)*

**Chris Bobbe** · 2023-09-13 03:02 UTC

Empirically, I get mark-as-read events ([`update_message_flags/add`](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#update_message_flags-add)) when there are unread messages in a stream and I unsubscribe from the stream.

When maintaining an unreads data structure, this behavior is convenient, since handling those events is a basic, obvious job of the data structure. (Convenient but unnecessary, I think; without it, one could still just handle the [unsubscribe-from-stream event](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#subscription-remove).)

As long as this is the behavior, I think it would be good to document it on the [`update_message_flags/add` event](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#update_message_flags-add).

**Chris Bobbe** · 2023-09-13 03:13 UTC

(For background, there's a reason why clients should make their data structure clear out messages' unread state on unsubscribing from the stream. It's because the server clears out the unread state in the database. If the user resubscribes to the stream, the client should match the server in not showing any as unread.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-13 16:36 UTC

That is certainly intended behavior and seems worth documenting.

At that time, the Zulip API docs as we know them didn't really exist yet — in particular the content of /api/register-queue was only added in 2020-08, in commit zulip/zulip@1d88c9e12e272441ddcd92ace1fe315cdf2ee0f5. Up until then, the doc comments in zulip-mobile's `src/api/` tree were the documentation of the Zulip API.

Like any documentation, the information was checked against the code (including its history, for old servers) when it was written. And like any documentation, it would have been a compatibility bug if we'd accidentally broken its promises.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-24 21:15 UTC

So I think the right way to think about this thread isn't that we were relying on something unverified that needed investigation. Rather it's that there was some important information that had been missed in a migration from one documentation system to another, and needed to be ported to the new one.

(And when doing so, certainly that's a good time to check to confirm that the guarantee hadn't been accidentally broken in the interim.)

A few questions that came up as I worked on the changes in that PR are with **Deprecated** notes in the API documentation in general. **Lauryn Menard** · 2023-09-20 13:20 UTC

I'm pretty sure all of the other updates I've done so far that have deprecated something in the API have been as part of some change to the backend code that was already being noted in the API changelog. **Lauryn Menard** · 2023-09-20 13:20 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-20 17:24 UTC

I don't think an API feature level for when something is deprecated is particularly important -- in theory, all that someone reading the docs need to know is that the thing is deprecated and what they should do instead. There's maybe some marginal value in hinting how long ago that decision was made, but ultimately we will be actually removing deprecated features when we're no longer supporting clients that rely on the behavior.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-24 21:26 UTC

I agree with Tim's reply on the value of a feature level in the "Deprecated" note on the description of the property/endpoint/etc.

I think it is useful, though, to have deprecations mentioned in /api/changelog . That's helpful because a client maintainer may periodically sweep through the changelog looking for updates they should take, and deprecations are one of the pieces of information that's especially helpful to flag there — because they represent opportunities to future-proof one's code.

Once it's in the changelog, then it's necessarily associated with some feature level. At that point I think it's natural and best to include that in the "Deprecated" note too, even though on its own that part is only marginally useful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-24 23:19 UTC

> **Feature level 177** * [`GET /messages`](/api/get-messages), [`GET /messages/matches_narrow`](/api/check-messages-match-narrow), [`POST /message/flags/narrow`](/api/update-message-flags-for-narrow), [`POST /register`](/api/register-queue): Added support for three [search/narrow filters](/api/constr …

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-24 23:20 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-24 23:48 UTC

Yeah, I think probably 80% of the way to having deprecations consistently noted in the changelog is just to make sure that when something new is introduced that causes something else to be deprecated, the deprecation gets mentioned in the changelog entry. And that the mention includes some word starting with "deprecat-", so that Ctrl+F highlights them.

There are some deprecations that don't involve anything new, though, as Lauryn mentioned — including the example that prompted this thread. So that makes a bit more interesting of a question.

And for the reason I gave above, I think it'd be good to include those in the changelog. Probably cleanest is to allocate a feature level for them, when there isn't anything else happening at the same time that they naturally go with, just so that each feature level is relatively coherent in what it's about. But when they happened in the past and we didn't do that, we can just note them as part of the next feature level.

In addition to a topic being muted or being not muted, a topic can be actively *un*muted. When it is, the topic and its messages should be treated as if the stream is not muted, regardless of the mute setting on the stream.

**Greg Price** · 2023-09-22 19:25 UTC

As the help center says:
> Zulip lets you mute topics and streams to avoid receiving notifications for messages you are not interested in. Muting a stream effectively mutes all topics in that stream. You can also manually **mute** a topic in an unmuted stream, or **unmute** a topic in a muted stream.

So the user's stream-level and topic-level choices ultimately combine to produce just a single state for each topic: the topic is ultimately either muted or not muted. (Plus there's the new/upcoming feature where it can be "followed", but a followed topic is in particular not muted.)

Well, that's up to the client, right? If a client does use that value, then the one it gets at /api/register-queue time is just a starting point — it's up to the client to update the value as needed in response to events.

We could deprecate the field, but I think it's probably better to use it, and to fix the bug discussed above as well as any other issues that are a reason not to use it.

I believe the field isn't *strictly* needed, in an information-theoretic sense — that the client can compute the right value based on the rest of the `unread_msgs` data together with other information like which streams are muted and the `user_topic` data. But it's a pretty salient number, one that may be useful even in a client that isn't implementing all the ins and outs of Zulip's features. So it's helpful to have it provided conveniently on a platter.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2023-09-25 18:40 UTC

> the client shouldn't need to do much to maintain […] the unread_msgs data structure

The unreads data structure has a more complicated job than just tracking what message IDs are unread. :smile: It has to track each message's location (including across stream/topic moves) and whether it's mentioned. The client has to be written against imperfect information from the server about the window of (50k) messages whose unread state is supposed to be conveyed—including cases where, at `/register` time, for some values of an unread message's mute state and mention state, [servers falsely and deliberately represent the message as read](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/register.3A.20.60unread_msgs.2Ementions.60/near/1645170), leaving clients wondering whether, with some cleverness, they can in fact maintain correctness for all possible transitions in that mute or mention state. (They can't, I think—unless maybe *those* transitions can come with explicit mark-as-read or -unread events too?) Sometime soon clients may have to [start tracking senders for each message](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/243-mobile-team/topic/inbox.20view.20on.20web/near/1639157). Clients that follow web's example should [incorporate message data fetched outside the event system](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/7585f87c64fe4d3ae035f873e2ff0dbcb8765607/web/src/message_fetch.js#L40-L42), exposing themselves to races/internal inconsistencies caused by poor Internet connection (particularly concerning for mobile clients). When there's an API implementation bug, the client has to make a note of it and what server versions it affects, and perhaps handle it specially. It has to do all of this while managing its own efficiency, with input from things like [careful timing measurements](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/pull/304#pullrequestreview-1628032624).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-25 19:09 UTC

The "move to unsubscribed stream" case (3) is a bit complex -- if it's moved to a private stream, we actually send a "deleted message" event to you, since that's how that operation works from a client perspective for that user -- but the bug is that we may not do the right thing for moving to an unsubscribed public stream. 

I haven't double-checked the code, but I think the bug in (3) is not that the server marks the messages as read but doesn't send the event: It's that the server is not marking those messages as read at all. So I see that as a server bug, not a protocol bug, and in theory fixing it isn't really a change to this API -- it's a fix to the business logic for when we decide to mark things as read.

So I just don't want us to write documentation that talks about some laundry list of features -- I want documentation that explains what the protocol is doing and gives examples that you can test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-25 19:13 UTC

And the protocol is that a client that just cares about maintaining the `Set` of message IDs that are unread that one is syncing is simple:
* New `message` event comes in with `unread` flag, client is supposed to track that as unread.
* New `delete_message` event comes in -- client needs to remember to remove the message from the set -- we don't send a duplicate `update_message_flags` event for this.
* New `update_message_flags` event comes in -- client needs to update the data structure to toggle the state of those IDs.

Now, the a full client has to do a bunch more work than that because it actually wants to know where the messages are, whether they also have the `mentioned` flag, which locations are muted/follows/unmuted, etc., and we send the data required to do those adjustments both here and in `update_message` events.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-25 19:16 UTC

Maybe another way to put it is that if we changed the product decision for whether messages sent by muted users can be unread or not, or added some new "block" feature that was kinda similar to muted users and also cleared the `unread_msgs` part of that business logic change -- in theory a client shouldn't need to change anything in correct `unread_msgs` syncing code, because the server would be changing the `unread` flag internally and sending `update_message_flags` or `delete_message` events or whatever as appropriate for the product decision.

(The client might still want to expose that new feature in the UI or whatnot, but this part of the protocol is intended to be that the server manages changes and notifies the client appropriately)

For example, when messages that were unread are moved to a stream where the user is not subscribed, the resulting change in message flags (and the corresponding `update_message_flags` event with flag `read`) may happen later than the message move itself."

**Tim** (from [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/27348#discussion_r1370605648)):
"In some code paths where expensive database operations are involved, a deferred work queue processor is used, which can in rare cases backlog, resulting in a delay. For example, when messages that were unread are moved to a stream where the user is not subscribed, the resulting change in message flags (and the corresponding `update_message_flags` event with flag `read`) uses such a queue processor and thus clients may receive events somewhat than they receive the message move event itself."

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-10-25 16:21 UTC

Note that we shouldn't end the updated event description with the list of examples as that will appear to be the same list as the event's properties.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 19:01 UTC

I think as a client author, the routine delay of hundreds of milliseconds is actually more significant than the rare delay due to a backlog (of I guess minutes or hours or more).

That's because hundreds of milliseconds is enough to cause visible glitchy behavior if the client doesn't handle it properly, and a routine glitch is a bigger impact than a rare behavior that's longer-lasting but still at the level of a glitch.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 19:05 UTC

So one version might be:

"In some cases, a change in message flags that's caused by another change may happen a short while after the original change, rather than simultaneously. For example, when messages that were unread are moved to a stream where the user is not subscribed, the resulting change in message flags (and the corresponding `update_message_flags` event with flag `read`) may happen later than the message move itself. The delay in that example is typically hundreds of milliseconds and can in rare cases be hours or longer."

i.e. adding the quantitative information of the scale of the delay.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 19:08 UTC

I'd prefer to find a wording we think is clear without talking about things like "a deferred work queue processor" — that feels like getting into server implementation details that a reader of the API docs shouldn't have to try to think through the meaning of.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-25 19:27 UTC

I would propose the following:

> So one version might be: "In some cases, a change in message flags that's caused by another change may happen a short while after the original change, rather than simultaneously. For example, when messages that were unread are moved to a stream where the user is not subscribed, the resulting change …

It is definitely a partial outage of the server if the delay is longer than a few minutes -- Zulip Cloud at least will page if a queue is ever more than a few minutes, and as best I can recall, that has never happened with this particular queue processor, so I don't think it makes sense for client developers to be thinking about longer than a few minutes here as a concrete possibility.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 19:29 UTC

Great, LGTM.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-10-27 10:20 UTC

#27348 has been updated for the revisions above, as well as other review feedback. Thanks for drafting that text @Tim Abbott and @Greg Price!

Also, integrated the feedback in #**api design>unreads: access to messages** to that same PR.

**James VL** · 2024-02-09 01:38 UTC

(correct me if this is the wrong stream)

I'm using the Zulip API to [send a message](https://zulip.com/api/send-message) via a non-interactive bot.

It's been working fine if I user a from-url-encoded. However, I just tried switched over to JSON as noticed that the endpoint expects to read for query params and not the body. In other words: it ignores the JSON payload in the actual body of the request and tells me I'm `"Missing 'type' argument"`.

(If I add the "type" argue to my query params, the error message moves on to the next parameter.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-09 02:07 UTC

We accept `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `multipart/form-data` request bodies, not `application/json`. If you have questions about exactly what the requests are expected to look like, the example `curl` commands are good for answering those.

**Greg Price** · 2024-02-09 21:13 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Does it have a proper issue write-up for what we want to do?

Good question. I'm not aware of one. I think the key things we want are:
* Explain the overall encoding of parameters in Zulip API requests:
  * The body should have the encoding `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `multipart/form-data`; mention the contrast with `application/json`, because that's the encoding many readers will implicitly assume is being used.
  * Those encodings themselves take each parameter's value as a (byte) string.
  * To encode the parameter values into strings:
    * Types documented as objects, arrays, booleans, or numbers are encoded with JSON.
    * When the type is documented as string, the encoding varies across the API: usually the string value is used literally, but for some parameters on some endpoints it's encoded as JSON. To find out for sure for a particular parameter, see the `curl` example in that endpoint's documentation.
* Then a worked example would probably go a long way in illustrating this, in particular for making concrete the difference between `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and `application/json`, and the difference between using a string value literally and encoding it as JSON.
  * /api/send-message could be good here: it's probably the number-one most common endpoint for someone to be wanting to use when they have this question, it's not too complicated, and it has both `to` where a stream name needs to be JSON-encoded and `topic` and `content` where the string value is used literally.

**Greg Price** · 2024-02-09 21:15 UTC

Probably this would be a new page, linked from the /api/rest "Overview" page and shown near it in the left nav, in the same way as "HTTP headers" and "Error handling".

**Greg Price** · 2024-02-09 21:18 UTC

For the example, in some past thread @Anders Kaseorg showed exactly what the HTTP request body looks like in each of the two encodings we accept and what it would look like in the often-mentioned one we don't. Hopefully that's one of the threads linked above… ah yes, [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/Unsubscribe.20documentation.20vs.20reality/near/1511881).

(I guess that's the two we accept but not `application/json`.)

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-06-28 20:42 UTC

> it has both `to` where a stream name needs to be JSON-encoded

It looks like that we have a discrepancy for `POST /messages` where `to` (as a query parameter in the body) can be encoded as a raw string when specifying a stream name, while the OpenAPI schema expects `application/json`.

 The change was added in 521471dcd9f181e038bd42fd7b1bb0a99554b075 to address #13836.

@Kenneth R ran into trouble when converting the endpoint to use `typed_endpoint` as the openapi validation tests fail due to the encoding mismatch. We could possibly address this by expressing the accepted encoding of `to` properly, or add special handling to typed_endpoint for this particular situation.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-28 20:44 UTC

(Handy linkifier for the API docs page: /api/send-message)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-06-28 21:38 UTC

The only thing that’s guaranteed to work there is the JSON encoding. We can’t document that `to` accepts a raw stream name, since the raw stream name might happen to collide with a valid JSON encoding of an unrelated JSON value, in which case it won’t work.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-06-28 22:03 UTC

It would be ideal if we can drop the ad-hoc fallback for raw strings eventually. Currently, the Python example on /api/send-message indicates support of a raw string ``"to": "Denmark",`.

Most query parameters typed as `str` aren't expected to be JSON-encoded, and clients might rely on that -- [python-zulip-api already does it](https://github.com/zulip/python-zulip-api/blob/868ce8f225b82f628c48284ac91feb4c2c6a48cc/zulip/zulip/__init__.py#L578).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-06-28 22:07 UTC

However, the deprecation process of the raw string handling behavior might not worth it for this endpoint alone, because something like #**api documentation>OpenAPI requestBody** could also resolve this.

What we can do now is suppress the error emerged from the schema validation, until we find the need/time to work on the full migration.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-29 00:23 UTC

Yeah this might be a thing not worth migrating in the current API vs. just planning to have it no longer be relevant once when we move to using `PostBody`

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-29 00:32 UTC

This is one of the small handful of places in the API that I'd expect to be most annoying to migrate, because sending a message is basically the top use case for a small ad-hoc bot.

So unlike the vast majority of our API migrations, where if mobile and terminal don't use it then we go ahead and change it, for this we'd have to worry about the long tail of integrations our users have built. Potentially including shell scripts run from cron jobs that nobody quite remembers where they run or where the code is, but they do count on seeing the automated messages they post.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-29 00:38 UTC

And for a bot of that kind, I'd expect the *most* likely thing for it to do is to send the stream name as a raw string.

The second most likely is to use a numeric stream ID. But for this sort of bot, I'd expect using the stream name to feel most natural.

When they do use the stream name… since we don't even clearly document (as discussed above) that it *can* be JSON, or that JSON is preferred, the author isn't even wrong to just try the raw string, and then to go with that when they see it works.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-03 20:50 UTC

Apparently we now have at least one endpoint that takes its payload as `application/json` instead of as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `multipart/form-data`: #**api documentation>JSON-encoded data in request body@2253966**

This is OK because it's not part of the normal Zulip server API, but instead the Zulip push service API (aka bouncer API), whose client implementations are Zulip servers rather than Zulip clients. (I'd like us to someday do the same for the Zulip server API too, but it should only be done in a coordinated way, as discussed in the linked message.)

So when we at some point get around to documenting this encoding layer of our API as discussed at #**api documentation>POST does not accept body@1734988**  above, we should include a bit about that exception, and then that endpoint can link there: #**api documentation>JSON-encoded data in request body@2254251**

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-04 19:17 UTC

I think what I'd be most excited to do here is look at whether we can make our request-parsing framework accept `application/json` across the whole API, and that documentation can be mainly explaining the legacy model.

(Hmm, as an aside, this comment is a bit puzzling because we do in fact rewrite the URLs in zulip-mobile :smile: — it's in `src/webview/js/rewriteHtml.js`:
```js
const inlineApiRoutes: $ReadOnlyArray<RegExp> = [
  '^/user_uploads/',
  '^/thumbnail$',
  '^/avatar/',
].map(r => new RegExp(r));

/**
 * Rewrite the source URLs of <img> elements under the given root, inclusive.
 *
 *   1. Make relative URLs absolute, with a path based on the Zulip realm rather
 *      than the document location.
 *   2. If the source URL names an endpoint known to require authentication,
 *      inject an API key into its query parameters.
 */
const rewriteImageUrls = (auth: Auth, element: Element | Document) => {
    // …

    // 2: Inject the API key where needed.
    if (isUrlOnRealm(fixedSrc, realm)) {
      if (inlineApiRoutes.some(regexp => regexp.test(fixedSrc.pathname))) {
        // Ideally we'd just use `searchParams`, but that was new in Chrome 51
        // (and Safari 10).
        const delimiter = fixedSrc.search ? '&' : '';
        fixedSrc.search += `${delimiter}api_key=${auth.apiKey}`;
      }
    }
```

I think that's not pertinent for the question of how to document things, though; the endpoint works how it works and that's what we want to document, regardless of the exact motivation that led us to build it that way.)

- `/users/me/subscriptions/{stream_id}` is the main API endpoint for changing channel settings, I think, and would be valuable to document for upcoming mobile work.

- `/dev_list_users` is a mobile development environment API that we should probably document for completeness of all mobile app interfaces.
- There's a few more miscellaneous ones not worth discussing for now.

*2024-06-17 to 2024-06-26 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/API.20wrappers.20docs.20responsibility/with/1829013)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-06-17 22:58 UTC

This applies generally to endpoints beyond the one mentioned in the original topic, so quoting here:

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Went ahead and meged, but yeah we there's definitely some work to be done on the docstrings/examples more broadly.
Clearly anyone could work on this (I see the notes for adding endpoint docs), but does anyone already have focus/time/skills planned for improving this kind of API documentation?

That is, would this be better suited to someone already working on API docs, perhaps with review from those using the API in that language? Or is this generally less of a priority except in certain circumstances, so fine for users of the wrappers in that language to pick up?

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-17 23:06 UTC

I think in general the strategy we should aim for is that for any given piece of the API, we maintain the docs in just one place, which is the main Zulip API docs.

So for example the doc for the endpoint involved in that PR is at /api/get-stream-email-address . The Python binding for that API endpoint should be a boring mechanical wrapper, so that there's no interesting information to say about it other than what's contained on that page; the reader should just be given that information.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-17 23:10 UTC

A low-effort version of this is to just give the reader a link to that page. Then the reader mentally translates what's on the page into their language's terms, according to the conventions of the bindings they're using.

That's what zulip-flutter does. For example for /api/fetch-api-key, [we have](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/3196263c45ef2fdd196e18012c9c064142c793db/lib/api/route/account.dart):
```dart
/// https://zulip.com/api/fetch-api-key
Future<FetchApiKeyResult> fetchApiKey(ApiConnection connection, {
  required String username,
  required String password,
}) {
  // …
}

// …
class FetchApiKeyResult {
  final String apiKey;
  final String email;
  final int? userId; // TODO(server-7)
```

Everything in those types corresponds in a totally boring way to what appears at /api/fetch-api-key . And then to learn more, in particular about the specific semantics of those parameters and response properties, the reader follows the link to /api/fetch-api-key.


This is also what zulip-mobile does, except that we have our own comments on various parts of the API mostly because we wrote those comments in the period before Zulip had good (or indeed any) API documentation.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-17 23:11 UTC

The aspirational version is that there should be complete docs on the bindings, and they're generated from the API docs. That's nice (compared to a link) because it means users see the docs in their IDE when looking at call sites, and so on.

I don't think anyone's currently planning to work on that in the near term, though.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-06-24 23:41 UTC

- Separate API docs could be 'inlined' into any present API wrappers [minimal aspirational version?]
- For more complex existing API wrappers, links to docs from code work fine (in place of inlined docs), as you indicated for zulip-flutter - and we also do this variously in zulip-terminal
- In the absence of a suitable API wrapper, then one can have wrappers directly inside a project (zulip-flutter, zulip-mobile), which can be straightforward, particularly with some automation (which I recall zulip-flutter had, at least?)
- With a suitable/baseline API wrapper (eg. the Python `zulip` for zulip-terminal), this provides a useful starting point - and we can either use the lower-level calls for new features, or eventually migrate away using it as a template

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:02 UTC

I think in an ideal world, we would be reworking `python-zulip-api` around static types. Fundamentally, it has a library API designed 10 years ago, pre-mypy and `dataclasses`, with mirroring tools and bots/integrations as the main use cases, not full-fledged clients that are going to use a large part of the API surface area.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:05 UTC

We do get from time to time hear positive feedback from users about how easy to use that system is, especially `zulip-send`, so I don't think `python-zulip-api` is a bad library, exactly. But it's definitely behind on modernization.

I think it would be potentially reasonable for folks working on the Terminal app to either look at taking over more aggressive maintenance of `python-zulip-api` and adding types where convenient while preserving backwards-compatibility.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:06 UTC

The library does provide some value via networking/authentication/backoff stuff, and I'd prefer that we be dogfooding Python bindings via the terminal app over writing a totally independent set of bindings that isn't intended to be published.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:07 UTC

But we're not in a place where it's logistically convenient to update the bindings when we merge API changes. It is possible that we will have the time during @Kunal Sharma's summer to do some sweeps of adding bindings for more of the API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:07 UTC

But one of the nice things about the current dictionary format is that it usually means nothing goes horribly wrong if we haven't updated the Python bindings for a new API feature, which can be the case with strongly typed API bindings.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 23:59 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> The library does provide some value via networking/authentication/backoff stuff

Absolutely. And just to be explicit because what I wrote may not have been clear on that:

(replying to Greg Price)
> A client using it might do about as well by just calling the more generic "make a request" functions directly.

those more-generic "make a request" functions that I meant were those provided by the library. I haven't spent real time with python-zulip-api, but I'm thinking of the methods analogous to zulip-flutter's `ApiConnection.send` and its slightly higher-level wrappers `ApiConnection.get`, `ApiConnection.post`, and so on:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/155895ae5d2a385dc628bf602083989c0cafad7a/lib/api/core.dart#L84-L148
which encode some knowledge of how to construct the URL to talk to, how to provide authentication, and in zulip-flutter's case also the information that's at /api/rest-error-handling (and that's discussed in [this parallel thread](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/client.20response.20types.20.28Python.2B.3F.29/near/1838192) today).

IIUC python-zulip-api doesn't currently handle the last of those three things, but in the glimpses I've taken it looked like it the per-endpoint methods were calling more-generic functions that handled those first two jobs.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-26 00:07 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> But one of the nice things about the current dictionary format is that it usually means nothing goes horribly wrong if we haven't updated the Python bindings for a new API feature, which can be the case with strongly typed API bindings.

I think the point where that starts happening is actually another step past having static types (though it might be the step one calls "strong" types).

Writing down some TypedDict-based types and annotating the bindings with those, for mypy to read, won't cause anything new to go wrong when the bindings are out of date, because it won't change anything that happens at runtime. The situation will be the same as it is in zulip-mobile, and as I assume it is in zulip-terminal: things might go wrong because a client application actively tries to do something with a given piece of data it expects is there, but the same thing would have gone wrong even if there weren't type annotations to help us track those expectations.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-26 00:07 UTC

The step beyond that is to start automatically validating that all the expected fields are there and have the expected types — like Zulip web is starting to do with Zod, and like zulip-flutter does with `package:json_serializable` as a necessary step for turning a map-from-string-to-unknown into a reasonably ergonomic Dart object. In Python that'd presumably be done with Pydantic, like the Zulip server now does with (many?) incoming request bodies.

At that later step, there is a runtime effect, and so an incompatible server change can potentially cause a problem up front even in situations where the program would have otherwise gotten away with it because it wouldn't have ended up using that part of the data.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-26 00:09 UTC

(In whatever way that validation is done, it'd be important to have it not try to check that there aren't *new* fields it didn't expect. Checking that would create routine incompatibility that didn't need to be there. But I assume any tool we might use for that purpose is capable of refraining from that check, at least optionally if not by default.)

*2024-06-25 to 2024-06-25 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/client.20response.20types.20.28Python.2B.3F.29/with/1838165)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-06-25 21:58 UTC

I didn't want to clutter #**api documentation>documenting error responses**, but based on recent discussion in that topic wanted to seek feedback on ways to formalize the client-side endpoint response data to include errors, which has been on my mind to include recently - at least in zulip-terminal, in Python.
(historically this could go to #**integrations**, but it feels more to be across #**api documentation** and #**api design**, as well as potentially app-facing)

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-06-25 21:58 UTC

The initial focus on Python (or otherwise) is not intended to indicate that language-specific wrappers/bindings/examples be included in documentation, particularly given #**api documentation>API wrappers docs responsibility**. Of course this could include some kind of manual typing along the lines of that below, on demand per-language. Alternatively I'm aware there was some experimentation with general automatic language bindings generation in the past; I don't believe that was successful, but perhaps generation of only data types would be feasible?

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-06-25 21:58 UTC

Anyhow, at a minimal level, feedback on a structure something like below would be appreciated:
```python
class ResponseBaseError(TypedDict):
    result: Literal["error"]
    msg: str

class ResponseSimpleError(ResponseBaseError):
    code: Literal["BAD_REQUEST", "AUTHENTICATION_FAILED"] # Literals for basic errors; BAD_REQUEST maybe split-out?

class ResponseRequestVariableMissingError(ResponseBaseError)
    code: Literal["REQUEST_VARIABLE_MISSING"]
    var_name: str  # extra data

# [Other more complex error types]

ResponseErrors = ResponseSimpleError | ResponseRequestVariableMissingError  # | ...

class ResponseSuccess(TypedDict):
    result: Literal["success"]
    # msg: Literal[""]  # deprecated (or generally unused)?

GeneralSuccessOrFailure = ResponseErrors | ResponseSuccess

class SomeEndpointSuccess(ResponseSuccess):
    ... # extra fields

SomeEndpointSuccessOrFailure = SomeEndpointSuccess  # | {set of possible failure errors}
```

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 22:15 UTC

IIRC the current behavior of the python-zulip-api bindings is that they return the whole response blob as a dict, so something like the `SomeEndpointSuccessOrFailure` in that outline.

I think the key thing I'd recommend there is that when a request gets an error, the method shouldn't return. It should throw. That seems like the behavior one normally expects in Python.

Then once it's doing that, when it does return there's no need to include `result: "success"` either.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 22:17 UTC

For how to model the exceptions to throw when the request gets an error, here's [what we have in zulip-flutter](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/155895ae5d2a385dc628bf602083989c0cafad7a/lib/api/exception.dart):
```dart
/// An error returned through the Zulip server API.
///
/// See API docs: https://zulip.com/api/rest-error-handling
class ZulipApiException extends ApiRequestException {

  /// The Zulip API error code returned by the server.
  final String code;

  /// The HTTP status code returned by the server.
  ///
  /// This is always in the range 400..499.
  final int httpStatus;

  /// The error's JSON data, if any, beyond the properties common to all errors.
  ///
  /// This consists of the properties other than `result`, `code`, and `msg`.
  ///
  /// For most types of errors, this will be empty.
  final Map<String, dynamic> data;
```

We've had something pretty similar in zulip-mobile for a number of years and I've been happy with it there; this has only slight tweaks relative to that.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 22:21 UTC

Then for each endpoint, you just write something like (adapted from your version above):
```py
class SomeEndpointResult(TypedDict):
  # … fields returned by this endpoint

def some_endpoint(…) -> SomeEndpointResult:
  # …
```

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 22:26 UTC

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> Alternatively I'm aware there was some experimentation with general automatic language bindings generation in the past; I don't believe that was successful, but perhaps generation of only data types would be feasible?

FWIW I think actually the data types are likely to be harder than the endpoints themselves for getting the generated bindings to be good.

(I initially wrote "likely to be the hardest part of getting …", but then thought again and realized that a harder part yet is compatibility with old servers, even recent old servers. Currently the information on how old servers differ from current servers is 100% expressed in prose descriptions, in those "Changes" notes we have all over the docs. Those work extremely well for human readers, but if we wanted to use them as input to generated bindings we'd have to totally rethink how they're expressed.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 22:31 UTC

Yeah that kind of multi-version-compatibility is not readily supported in OpenAPI AFAIK. 

And while I've not done an exhaustive survey, the anecdotal reaction that I get when I mention `openapi-generator` to other people with complex APIs using OpenAPI is that they've not been able to figure out how to make it produce something they were happy with. So I'm not optimistic about that being successful anytime soon.

I'm pretty sure the idea is that all the messages in the list are from the same conversation. The fields `message_type`, `stream_id`, `topic` don't make a lot of sense unless the messages are always either

Currently, as per the [docs for `near` operator](https://zulip.com/help/search-for-messages#search-by-message-id):

But the actual functioning of the operator is as described in the comment in `message_view.js`:

// We attempt the match the stream and topic with that of the
// message in case the message was moved after the link was
// created. This ensures near / id links work and will redirect
// correctly if the topic was moved (including being resolved).
```

So, this would mean `near` operator would only show messages around the id if it is moved. Else, it would show the conversation corresponding to remaining narrow. I guess this needs to be added to the docs?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 17:03 UTC

The logic in `message_view.js` does two things:
- If we have a copy of the message in cache, check if it has moved, and if so, navigate to the post-move location.
- If we don't fetch it from the server to get it into cache and do the same as the above.

That is entirely client-side logic for implementing those aspects of the `near` behavior. 

I think it would be reasonable to document that in the API documentation, but it should be very clearly explained as recommended client implementation details.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 23:50 UTC

And then there's an additional effect that a `near` operator has, which is purely client-side. This effect goes in a similar direction to the effect we later designed for `with`, but it works differently.

That effect is, as (replying to Tim Abbott)
> - If we have a copy of the message in cache, check if it has moved, and if so, navigate to the post-move location. - If we don't fetch it from the server to get it into cache and do the same as the above.

But here, "has moved" is meant literally: we actually look through the edit history of the message object, we  look to see if it previously existed within the narrow the rest of the filters specify, and if so then we go to where the message is now.

This contrasts with `with` where we go to the conversation the message is in now regardless of whether it previously existed somewhere else.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 23:51 UTC

Well, it depends on what "around" means. If you edit that URL to have `/near/1`, it'll show your first messages from that DM conversation. If you edit it to have `/near/99999999999999`, it'll show the latest. With `/near/1908077`, it'll show the messages whose IDs are right around 1908077.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 23:52 UTC

So it's not messages that are "around" that one in the sense that they live in the same conversation. But they're "around" it in time, or in their message ID.

> I believe neither zulip-web nor zulip-mobile sorts the returned result.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-08-12 03:05 UTC

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-08-12 03:08 UTC

**Khader Khudair** · 2024-08-12 09:00 UTC

Ok, I have taken a look into server, I think it does sort topics by recency.
To come up with this conclusion:

I've taken a look at [zproject/urls.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zproject/urls.py)..
Which indicates that the rest endpoint returns the result of `get_topics_backend`
```python
    rest_path(
        "users/me/<int:stream_id>/topics", GET=(get_topics_backend, {"allow_anonymous_user_web"})
    ),
```

Looking at `get_topics_backend` in [zerver/views/streams.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/views/streams.py)...
we can find that the result would always be one of `get_topic_history_for_public_stream` or `get_topic_history_for_stream`

```python
@typed_endpoint
def get_topics_backend(
    request: HttpRequest,
    maybe_user_profile: UserProfile | AnonymousUser,
    *,
    stream_id: PathOnly[NonNegativeInt],
) -> HttpResponse:
    if not maybe_user_profile.is_authenticated:
        is_web_public_query = True
        user_profile: UserProfile | None = None
    else:
        is_web_public_query = False
        assert isinstance(maybe_user_profile, UserProfile)
        user_profile = maybe_user_profile
        assert user_profile is not None

    if is_web_public_query:
        realm = get_valid_realm_from_request(request)
        stream = access_web_public_stream(stream_id, realm)
        result = get_topic_history_for_public_stream(
            realm_id=realm.id, recipient_id=assert_is_not_none(stream.recipient_id)
        )

    else:
        assert user_profile is not None

        (stream, sub) = access_stream_by_id(user_profile, stream_id)

        assert stream.recipient_id is not None
        result = get_topic_history_for_stream(
            user_profile=user_profile,
            recipient_id=stream.recipient_id,
            public_history=stream.is_history_public_to_subscribers(),
        )

    return json_success(request, data=dict(topics=result))
```
Finally, looking at [zerver/lib/topic.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/topic.py)..
We can see both `get_topic_history_for_public_stream` and `get_topic_history_for_stream` do indeed order results (both use `ORDER BY max("zerver_message".id) DESC`)

```python
def get_topic_history_for_public_stream(realm_id: int, recipient_id: int) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    # Uses index: zerver_message_realm_recipient_subject
    # Note that this is *case-sensitive*, so that we can display the
    # most recently-used case (in generate_topic_history_from_db_rows)
    query = """
    SELECT
        "zerver_message"."subject" as topic,
        max("zerver_message".id) as max_message_id
    FROM "zerver_message"
    WHERE (
        "zerver_message"."realm_id" = %s AND
        "zerver_message"."recipient_id" = %s
    )
    GROUP BY (
        "zerver_message"."subject"
    )
    ORDER BY max("zerver_message".id) DESC
    """
    cursor.execute(query, [realm_id, recipient_id])
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    cursor.close()

    return generate_topic_history_from_db_rows(rows)


def get_topic_history_for_stream(
    user_profile: UserProfile, recipient_id: int, public_history: bool
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    if public_history:
        return get_topic_history_for_public_stream(user_profile.realm_id, recipient_id)

    cursor = connection.cursor()
    # Uses index: zerver_message_realm_recipient_subject
    # Note that this is *case-sensitive*, so that we can display the
    # most recently-used case (in generate_topic_history_from_db_rows)
    query = """
    SELECT
        "zerver_message"."subject" as topic,
        max("zerver_message".id) as max_message_id
    FROM "zerver_message"
    INNER JOIN "zerver_usermessage" ON (
        "zerver_usermessage"."message_id" = "zerver_message"."id"
    )
    WHERE (
        "zerver_usermessage"."user_profile_id" = %s AND
        "zerver_message"."realm_id" = %s AND
        "zerver_message"."recipient_id" = %s
    )
    GROUP BY (
        "zerver_message"."subject"
    )
    ORDER BY max("zerver_message".id) DESC
    """
    cursor.execute(query, [user_profile.id, user_profile.realm_id, recipient_id])
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    cursor.close()

    return generate_topic_history_from_db_rows(rows)

```

## provide an explicit format for `realm_user.date_joined`

*2024-11-12 to 2024-11-13 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/provide.20an.20explicit.20format.20for.20.60realm_user.2Edate_joined.60/with/1979735)*

**Sayed Mahmood Sayedi** · 2024-11-12 15:22 UTC

At the [register-queue](https://zulip.com/api/register-queue) docs page, the documentation for `realm_user.date_joined` reads as follows: ***"The time the user account was created."***, which is not quite explanatory specifically about the time zone. After logging it, it seems to be in `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm+00:00` format.

**Greg Price** · 2024-11-12 23:41 UTC

Thanks for starting the thread!

It'd be good to have the format documented clearly. As it stands, it sounds like it could be a number of seconds since the epoch (the type is string, but it could be stringified), or a date-and-time in some other format.

The two key points I'd want written down are:
* It's in ISO 8601 format.
* It has an explicit time zone (that `+00:00` suffix).

This came up [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/pull/886/#discussion_r1815899882) on #F886, where we're parsing these in the Flutter app.

In particular if these were to be expressed *without* an explicit time zone — like "2024-11-12T23:38:51", instead of "2024-11-12T23:38:51+00:00" — and just implicitly meant as UTC, then the off-the-shelf `DateTime.parse` from the Dart stdlib would interpret that string, reasonably enough, as meaning the client's local time. Which we could also deal with (it's a string, we can parse it however we need to) but we'd need explicit logic to do so.

**Sayed Mahmood Sayedi** · 2024-11-13 02:11 UTC

Absolutely.

One thing to point out is that it seems not to include the seconds part, so `2024-11-12T23:38+00:00` instead of `2024-11-12T23:38:51+00:00`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-11-13 02:27 UTC

Note that logged-out spectators only see `YYYY-MM-DD`, and for logged-in visitors we recently changed the precision from microseconds to minutes (#31190).

**Greg Price** · 2024-11-13 03:37 UTC

Hmm yeah. For those logged-out spectators with just the date, I'm guessing there's no `+00:00` at the end.

The time zone is less relevant for those, though still not meaningless — the user joined in the 24-hour period described by that date in UTC, and not necessarily in the overlapping 24-hour period described by that date with any nonzero offset to UTC.

**Greg Price** · 2024-11-13 03:40 UTC

Our immediate use case in #F886 is for the `date_joined` of the self-user, in order to determine whether they have the "full member" role in the case where that affects a permission. So any wrinkles for logged-out spectators don't need to be implemented right now, but @Sayed Mahmood Sayedi the `DateTime.parse` should get a comment pointing at this thread so that we know those wrinkles are there in a future where we go reuse that logic for a more general situation.

**Sayed Mahmood Sayedi** · 2024-11-13 05:56 UTC

> the `DateTime.parse` should get a comment pointing at this thread so...

Done.

The interesting constraint here is that we have an unusual habit of including the full change history for our API in the individual descriptions of parts of our API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-03 17:28 UTC

This choice is very important to the actual way we work; I actually gave an invited talk on the topic at a FHIR conference last year (I wonder if the video's up? **Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-03 17:38 UTC

Now a thing that a lot of modern projects try to do around their API documentation is try to make their OpenAPI specs be generated from the implementation itself -- say, you add docstrings to the Pedantic type definitions and the view function definitions, use plumbing like we have in `test_openapi.py` to do the mappings, and glue those together into your generated OpenAPI spec.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-03 17:41 UTC

That approach has trade-offs:
- Some review process changes required -- it no longer jumps out at a reviewer that an API change has occurred, and we need to check its discussion in #**api design** for approval, etc. Probably solvable by checking the generated OpenAPI specs into `Git` so documentation changes are right there in the diffs, or a GitHub action to post the diff to the generated spec files, depending how we want to manage it.
- It often becomes harder to make the documentation say precisely what you want it to say, if there are limitations in your auto-generation tooling.

We're mostly pretty good about that but sometimes have slips like this one. It'd be a good small docs bug to fix.

The rule is that when you're only concerned with the latest server, you can stop reading any description as soon as you get to "**Changes:**". Then on top of that, they're in reverse chronological order; so if you're only concerned with servers back to some version, you can stop as soon as you see a "**Changes:**" item describing an older version.

We don't seem to mention how `mandatory_topics` realm setting interact with the [`send-message` endpoint](https://zulip.com/api/send-message#parameter-topic).

~~~ py
def get_spoiler_content(elem: Element) -> SpoilerContentNode:
    restrict(elem, "div", "class", "aria-hidden")
    ensure_class(elem, "spoiler-content")
    ensure_attribute(elem, "aria-hidden", "true")
    aria_attribute_comes_first = list(elem.attrib.keys())[0] == "aria-hidden"
    return SpoilerContentNode(
        children=get_child_nodes(elem, ignore_newlines=True),
        aria_attribute_comes_first=aria_attribute_comes_first,
    )


def get_spoiler_header(elem: Element) -> SpoilerHeaderNode:
    restrict(elem, "div", "class")
    ensure_class(elem, "spoiler-header")
    return SpoilerHeaderNode(children=get_child_nodes(elem, ignore_newlines=True))


def get_spoiler_node(elem: Element) -> SpoilerNode:
    restrict(elem, "div", "class")
    ensure_class(elem, "spoiler-block")
    header_elem, content_elem = get_two_children(elem)
    header = get_spoiler_header(header_elem)
    content = get_spoiler_content(content_elem)
    return SpoilerNode(header=header, content=content)
~~~

**Lauryn Menard** · 2025-08-07 16:09 UTC

So, I feel like the new tool for adding changelog entries for API updates has been really great in that there's a lot less friction when merging various PRs with API changes.

But I also feel like there's been a reduced amount of review of the rendered API documentation that's being done as part of the PR review process.

And some of that is on me as the maintainer of the API documentation, but I feel like some of that is also the process of these changes getting merged.

It's probably fine in cases where we need to get the PR changes merged quickly to keep development of a feature moving forward for an API documentation review to be done after a PR is merged. But we should have a way to flag me for an API docs review to happen / get on my to-do list post-merge.

## JSON-encoded data in request body

*2025-09-03 to 2025-09-03 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/JSON-encoded.20data.20in.20request.20body/with/2253966)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-03 14:56 UTC

We have `POST /remotes/push/e2ee/notify` endpoint on bouncer which accepts a JSON-encoded payload in request body.

We have `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for other endpoints.

CZO search for why we're not preferring `application/json` instead of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`resulted in a [thread where @Greg Price said](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/OpenAPI.20requestBody/near/1622599) :
> The API's mixture of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with JSON is definitely a mess, and it'd be good to clean it up and use all JSON.

> I think I would not want us to start having new endpoints do something different — I'd prefer to hold off on that until we have a plan for migrating everything (or at least everything-but-a-few-exceptions) to support all JSON. Even then, it's probably better if new endpoints support both forms for as long as all the existing endpoints do.

> The thing is that if any given client has to support talking to some endpoints in all-JSON form at the same time as other endpoints are in `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with our existing mixture of sometimes using JSON inside the values, that state is even messier than the status quo.

Since clients don't need to interact with this endpoint, it's acceptable to use `application/json` here.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-03 14:57 UTC

Planning to document the JSON payload in this way, let me know if we have any other plan:
[Screenshot 2025-09-03 at 7.17.41 PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/27/Id-zVKIhddIilTuorXXOkvvw/Screenshot-2025-09-03-at-7.17.41PM.png)

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-03 20:33 UTC

Yeah, having this endpoint differ from the rest by taking the whole body as JSON is fine.

Thanks for digging up that previous message, and I agree its reasoning doesn't apply here. Basically that's because this is part of a different API implemented by a different set of clients: this is the Zulip bouncer API (or Zulip push service API) and its clients are Zulip servers. The API we usually talk about is the Zulip server API, whose clients are Zulip clients.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-10 00:32 UTC

What's the behavior of the narrow filter `is:muted`?

It exists according to /api/construct-narrow , and is documented a bit at https://zulip.com/help/mute-a-topic . It's supposed to match "muted messages". But which are those?

In particular, what does it do with messages that are in a muted channel, in a topic with no visibility policy of its own? The behavior of the Zulip message feeds is that those messages *don't* appear in the combined feed (they're muted), but they *do* appear in the channel feed (so they're effectively unmuted there). Does `is:muted` treat those as muted or unmuted? Does its behavior change depending on whether there's also a channel filter?

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-10 00:33 UTC

My motivation here is that I'd ideally like to be able to express a narrow which corresponds to the messages that the client actually shows in a given message feed, i.e. excluding those which the client filters out because they're muted.

That would be useful for fixing the issue described at #**mobile>mark-read and muted topics/channels@2349170**, by sending that narrow in a request to /api/update-message-flags-for-narrow .

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-10 00:33 UTC

`is:muted` as a search operator matches messages that are in a muted topic or channel.

## OpenAPI refactors for better code generation

**elle** · 2026-01-15 22:49 UTC

hello all,

I started some refactor work in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37062 to improve code generation using the reference [openapi-generator-cli](https://github.com/OpenAPITools/openapi-generator-cli) tool.

For generating Rust client code, a number of changes are needed just to get the tool to generate code (the current changes in #37062).

However, I would also like to make wider changes to the OpenAPI spec to improve the code generation even more. Currently, the generated code includes a lot of boilerplate, and isn't able to decode the proper data structure in a number of places. This looks to be originating from inline structure definitions in the OpenAPI spec.

It would also be nice to get the spec to the point of being able to pass `openapi-generator-cli`'s specification validator (it does not currently).

[progenitor](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/progenitor) is another tool to generate at least Rust client code. Ideally, I would like to have the spec work with both tools. Though, `openapi-generator-cli` takes precedence, and I suspect once things are working there other tools will also be happy.

I'm looking for community feedback on a good way forward making the necessary spec refactors.

Thanks for reading (apologies for the info dump)

> Event sent to users who can administer a bot user when the bot is configured. Clients may also receive a `realm_user` event that for changes in public data about the bot (name, etc.).

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-02-26 20:14 UTC

#**api design>device records** for background on this one.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-02-26 20:15 UTC

One thing that I'm not sure about is whether there should be a way for clients to delete these records as part of an API key change / deletion. Maybe we want the server to automatically delete these records when you rotate your API key (or in the future, delete a given API key)?

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-27 01:30 UTC

Hmm yeah, good question.

In the future with #17939 (separate API keys per device), we'll want deleting one of these device records to be synonymous with revoking the associated API key.

For device records that don't have their own API key (which includes all device records today, before #17939), I think the right model is to think of them as all being attached to the user's single per-user API key. So if the user rotates/revokes their API key, then those device records should all get removed.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-27 01:35 UTC

Because the API key was revoked, the client will get a 401 response the next time it tries to get a new data snapshot; it'll recognize the user has been logged out, and delete its local record of that account so that the user logs in afresh if they want to keep using that device with that account. That new login will create a fresh device record on the server anyway.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-27 01:36 UTC

Meanwhile, for the mobile client side of this API change: I'll include it in one of the ongoing series of PRs for #F1764.

export async function upload_file(file: File) {
    const url = new URL("/api/v1/user_uploads", realm_data.url);
    const formData = new FormData();

    formData.append("FILE", file);

    const headers = get_headers();

    const response = await fetch(url, {
        method: "POST",
        headers,
        body: formData,
    });
    console.log(response);
    const data = await response.json();
    console.log(data);
}

function get_headers() {
    const auth = btoa(`${self_creds.email}:${self_creds.api_key}`);
    const auth_header = `Basic ${auth}`;
    return { Authorization: auth_header };
}
~~~

The name absolutely doesn't matter -- it's just looking for one file upload object:
```python
def upload_file_backend(request: HttpRequest, user_profile: UserProfile) -> HttpResponse:
    if len(request.FILES) == 0:
        raise JsonableError(_("You must specify a file to upload"))
    if len(request.FILES) != 1:
        raise JsonableError(_("You may only upload one file at a time"))

    [user_file] = request.FILES.values()
```

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-05 20:50 UTC

We don't really have a "profile summary" UI as distinct from the full profile page. The one thing we do with that `display_in_profile_summary` flag is therefore this:
```dart
  static List<CustomProfileField> _sortCustomProfileFields(List<CustomProfileField> initialCustomProfileFields) {
    // TODO(server): The realm-wide field objects have an `order` property,
    //   but the actual API appears to be that the fields should be shown in
    //   the order they appear in the array (`custom_profile_fields` in the
    //   API; our `realmFields` array here.)  See chat thread:
    //     https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/custom.20profile.20fields/near/1382982
    //
    // We go on to put at the start of the list any fields that are marked for
    // displaying in the "profile summary".  (Possibly they should be at the
    // start of the list in the first place, but make sure just in case.)
    final displayFields = initialCustomProfileFields.where((e) => e.displayInProfileSummary == true);
    final nonDisplayFields = initialCustomProfileFields.where((e) => e.displayInProfileSummary != true);
    return displayFields.followedBy(nonDisplayFields).toList();
```

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-05 20:50 UTC

So I think no mobile update needed.

*2026-03-14 to 2026-03-26 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/anchor.20in.20get.20messages.20response/with/2409667)*

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2026-03-14 16:56 UTC

https://zulip.com/api/get-messages#response
I wonder if the `anchor` in the return values docmentation needs some revision.
The `anchor=date` parameter also returns a computed message id that is closest to the date.
But we get `0` and `10000000000000000`, for `anchor=oldest` and `anchor=newest` respectively.

```spoiler Responses that I got on local testing

When using `anchor=oldest` in the request parameters, we get `0` for the `anchor` in the response.
````
$ curl -sSX GET -G https://chat.zulip.org/api/v1/messages \
  -u email:foobar\
  --data-urlencode anchor=oldest \
  --data-urlencode num_before=0 \
  --data-urlencode num_after=1 \
  --data-urlencode allow_empty_topic_name=true \
  --data-urlencode 'narrow=[{"operator":"stream","operand":"design"}]'
{"result":"success","msg":"","messages":[...],"found_anchor":false,"found_oldest":true,"found_newest":false,"history_limited":false,"anchor":0}
````

For `anchor=newest`, it's `10000000000000000`

````
$ curl -sSX GET -G https://chat.zulip.org/api/v1/messages \
  -u email:foobar\
  --data-urlencode anchor=newest \
  --data-urlencode num_before=1 \
  --data-urlencode num_after=0 \
  --data-urlencode allow_empty_topic_name=true \
  --data-urlencode 'narrow=[{"operator":"stream","operand":"design"}]'
{"result":"success","msg":"","messages":[...],"found_anchor":false,"found_oldest":false,"found_newest":true,"history_limited":false,"anchor":10000000000000000}
````

For `anchor=date` with the `anchor_date` in the future, we get the newest message_id as the `anchor` in the response.

````
(zulip-server) ➜  zulip git:(date-search-operator) ✗ curl -sSX GET -G https://chat.zulip.org/api/v1/messages \
  -u email:foobar\
  --data-urlencode anchor=date \
  --data-urlencode anchor_date=2050-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --data-urlencode num_before=1 \
  --data-urlencode num_after=0 \
  --data-urlencode allow_empty_topic_name=true \
  --data-urlencode 'narrow=[{"operator":"stream","operand":"design"}]'
{"result":"success","msg":"","messages":[...],"found_anchor":true,"found_oldest":false,"found_newest":false,"history_limited":false,"anchor":2409545}
````

Same for a super old `anchor_date` with `anchor=date`:

````
$ curl -sSX GET -G https://chat.zulip.org/api/v1/messages \
  -u email:asdf\
  --data-urlencode anchor=date \
  --data-urlencode anchor_date=1960-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --data-urlencode num_before=1 \
  --data-urlencode num_after=0 \
  --data-urlencode allow_empty_topic_name=true \

{"result":"success","msg":"","messages":[....],"found_anchor":true,"found_oldest":true,"found_newest":false,"history_limited":false,"anchor":150417}
````

```
